SampleSizeCalc: A Comprehensive Guide to Sample Size Determination in Clinical Research

Portos (Yishan) Wang and Bingxin Cai

2026-11-11

Source: vignettes/clinical-guide-en.Rmd
clinical-guide-en.Rmd

Introduction: The Lifeblood of Clinical Research

For clinical investigators, calculating sample size is often the most critical step when preparing grant proposals or IRB submissions.

Underpowered trials risk false-negative findings (\(P > 0.05\)), wasting research grants and patient effort. Conversely, overpowered trials waste resources and expose unnecessary subjects to experimental risks.

The SampleSizeCalc package supports the designs illustrated in 52 clinical scenarios below. Each example explains the population, study procedures, endpoint, planning assumptions, and how the result translates into recruitment.

These are teaching protocols. Except where a published numerical example is explicitly identified, clinical effects, standard deviations, event rates, and margins are illustrative assumptions. The methodological reference supports the formula; it does not establish those clinical inputs. A real protocol should document the source population, endpoint definition, follow-up window, and uncertainty of each planning input.

Numerical interpretations are evaluated from the R result objects when the site is built. Some diagnostic branches convert an unrounded requirement to a screening total; operational recruitment should also respect integer case and control quotas. Default reports contain the plain-text formula, LaTeX source, calculation process, and references.

Plain-English Glossary of Statistical Terms

  • \(\alpha\) (Type I Error / False Positive): The probability of declaring a treatment effective when it truly is not — the “probability of convicting an innocent drug” (conventionally 0.05).
  • \(\text{Power} = 1 - \beta\) (True Positive Detection): The probability of catching a true effect when it exists — the “probability of catching the real culprit” (routinely 0.80 or 0.90).
  • Continuous vs. Binary Endpoints: Continuous measures numerical values (systolic BP drop in mmHg, fasting glucose in mmol/L); binary measures event status (eradicated vs. not, cured vs. not).
  • Two-Sided vs. One-Sided: Two-sided tests for differences in either direction (classical RCTs); one-sided tests for non-inferiority and directional superiority.
  • Dropout Rate (\(d\)): Inflation formula \(N_{\text{screen}} = \lceil N / (1 - d) \rceil\).

Unified Syntax: The Three-Axis Function calculate()

\[\texttt{calculate(design, task, outcome, ...)}\]

  • Axis 1 design: what type of study? ("rct", "paired", "cohort", "caseControl", "diagAccuracy", "diagAUC", "singleArmPhaseII", "bioequivalence", "clusterRCT", …)
  • Axis 2 task: what scientific question? ("test" hypothesis testing, "estimate" CI precision, "noninferiority", "superiority", "equivalence")
  • Axis 3 outcome: how is the endpoint measured? ("mean", "proportion", "survival", "auc", "rate", "ordinal", "lr", "correlation", "events")

Printing a result shows the formula in plain text and LaTeX, the calculation process, and references. summary() also lists all inputs, design axes, and recorded adjustments.

Chapter 1: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs)

1.1 Two Independent Means (Continuous Endpoint)

  • Population and decision: A cardiology service plans a blinded, parallel, 1:1 randomized trial in adults aged 40–75 whose background antihypertensive treatment is stable, comparing an add-on study drug with add-on placebo.
  • Procedures and endpoint: At baseline and week 12, use the same protocol to average repeated seated BP readings. The primary outcome is baseline minus week-12 systolic BP, so a larger positive change means greater improvement; each patient supplies one change score.
  • Planning inputs: Assume mean reductions of 10 and 12 mmHg and a common change-score SD of 3 mmHg. These map to mean1, mean2, and sd; the SD of baseline BP is not interchangeable with the SD of change. Verify these assumptions using comparable pilot or external data.
  • Why this design: The question is whether two independent mean changes differ, using two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. The targeted between-group difference is 2 mmHg, distinct from either group’s reduction from baseline.
  • Formula: \[n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2}\right)^2\] Chow, Shao, Wang & Lokhnygina (2017), Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.), CRC Press.
res_1_1 <- calculate("rct", "test", "mean", mean1 = 10, mean2 = 12, sd = 3, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_1)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Two independent samples, mean comparison"
#> • Sample size per group: 37
#> • Total sample size: 74
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = 2 * ((Z_alpha/2 + Z_beta) * sd / (mean1 - mean2))^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = 2\left(\frac{Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}}{\delta}\right)^2 = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2}\right)^2$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: mu1 = mu2 vs H1: mu1 != mu2 (two-sided alpha =
#> 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Calculate mean difference delta = |mu1 - mu2| = |10 - 12| = 2; common
#> SD sigma = 3.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96 (for two-sided alpha =
#> 0.05), Z_beta = 0.8416 (for power = 0.80).
#> • Step 4: Compute initial sample size via normal approximation: n0 = 2 *
#> ((Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta) * sigma / delta)^2 = 2 * ((1.96 + 0.8416) * 3 / 2)^2 =
#> 35.32.
#> • Step 5: Refine via exact two-sample Student's t-test power iteration
#> (accounting for degrees of freedom df = 2n - 2).
#> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 37 per group, total sample size N = 74.
#> Reference:
#> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Chapter 3 (Comparing Means), Section 3.2.1 two-sample parallel design, Eq 3.11 (p. 48; the Student t refinement is Table 3.2, p. 49).
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Eq 5.4, p. 69 (same formula with the Student t correction term).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 37 analyzable patients per arm, 74 total. The report shows the normal approximation of about 35.32 per arm before the noncentral t calculation and rounding. If 10% are expected to lack the primary endpoint, plan 42 per arm (84 total); this additional adjustment is not included in the RCT result.

The four report components

Component Console label Result field
Plain-text formula Formula (plain text) formula
LaTeX source Formula (LaTeX) formula_latex
Calculation process Calculation process calculation_steps (alias calculation)
References Reference reference 
res_1_1$formula
cat(res_1_1$formula_latex)
cat(res_1_1$calculation_steps, sep = "\n")
cat(res_1_1$reference)

The R console displays copyable LaTeX source. To typeset it in R Markdown, use cat(res_1_1$formula_latex) in a chunk with results = "asis". The reporting guide includes an executed example and instructions for saving the report.

1.2 Two Independent Proportions (Binary Endpoint)

  • Population and decision: A gastroenterology trial enrolls adults with confirmed H. pylori infection who are eligible for either of two 14-day regimens, with recent antibiotic use and previous eradication failure handled by prespecified eligibility rules.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Determine eradication with a standardized urea breath test in a fixed post-treatment window. Define medication restrictions, invalid tests, and repeat assessments in advance; improvement in symptoms at treatment completion is not the eradication endpoint.
  • Planning inputs: Illustrative rates are p1 = 0.85 and p2 = 0.70, an absolute difference of 15 percentage points. Actual sources must match treatment history, resistance setting, and the timing and definition of eradication.
  • Why this design: Different patients form the two groups, so use independent proportions with two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. Prespecify how nonadherence and missing follow-up enter the analysis.
  • Formula (Fleiss asymptotic): \[n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{2\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_2)^2}\] Fleiss, Tytun & Ury (1980), Biometrics 36(2), 343-346.
res_1_2 <- calculate("rct", "test", "proportion", p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.70, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_2)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Two independent proportions"
#> • Sample size per group: 121
#> • Total sample size: 242
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = (Z_a/2 * sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_b * sqrt(p1*(1-p1)+p2*(1-p2)))^2 /
#> (p1-p2)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{2\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)}\right]^2}{(p_1 - p_2)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: p1 = p2 vs H1: p1 != p2 (two-sided alpha =
#> 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Compute pooled proportion: p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2 = (0.85 + 0.70) / 2
#> = 0.775.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Compute Fleiss formula numerator components:
#> Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) = 1.1575; Z_beta*sqrt(p1(1-p1)+p2(1-p2)) =
#> 0.4889.
#> • Step 5: Calculate unrounded sample size per group: n = (1.1575 + 0.4889)^2 /
#> (0.85 - 0.70)^2 = 120.47.
#> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 121 per group, total sample size N = 242.
#> Reference:
#> Primary (formula as implemented, without continuity correction): Fleiss, J. L., Tytun, A., & Ury, H. K. (1980). A simple approximation for calculating sample sizes for comparing independent proportions. Biometrics, 36(2), 343-346.
#> 
#> With continuity correction: Casagrande, J. T., Pike, M. C., & Smith, P. G. (1978). An improved approximate formula for calculating sample sizes for comparing two binomial distributions. Biometrics, 34(3), 483-494.
#> 
#> Book: Fleiss, J. L., Levin, B., & Paik, M. C. (2003). Statistical methods for rates and proportions (3rd ed.). Wiley.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 121 patients per arm, 242 total. Allowing for 10% missing primary endpoints gives 135 per arm and 270 total; the analysis population and missing-data strategy still require explicit definitions.

1.3 Survival Analysis (Log-Rank Test Events)

  • Population and decision: An oncology group plans a 1:1 randomized trial in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer patients eligible for both study regimens, with follow-up measured from randomization.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Specify overall survival as the primary outcome, with death from any cause as the event and last confirmed survival as the censoring date. Progression is not an overall-survival event; a progression-free survival design needs its own event definition and assumptions.
  • Planning inputs: Assume proportional hazards, hr = 0.70, experimental allocation pE = 0.50, two-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. A hazard ratio is not the ratio of two fixed-time death probabilities.
  • Why this design: First determine the number of deaths required. Accrual duration, additional follow-up, survival distributions, and losses then determine what fraction of recruited patients will contribute an event and when analysis is feasible.
  • Formula (Schoenfeld): \[E = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2}{p_E(1 - p_E)[\ln(HR)]^2}\] Schoenfeld (1983), Biometrics 39(2), 499-503.
res_1_3 <- calculate("rct", "test", "survival", hr = 0.70, pE = 0.50, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_3)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Survival (log-rank)"
#> • Events needed: 247
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `E = (Z_a/2 + Z_b)^2 / (pE*(1-pE)*log(HR)^2)`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$E = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2}{p_E(1-p_E)[\ln(HR)]^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State survival parameters: Hazard Ratio HR = 0.70, experimental arm
#> allocation pE = 0.50 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Compute log hazard ratio: ln(HR) = ln(0.70) = -0.3567.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Apply Schoenfeld formula: E = (Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta)^2 / [pE * (1 -
#> pE) * (ln HR)^2] = (1.96 + 0.8416)^2 / [0.50 * 0.50 * (-0.3567)^2] = 246.79.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target events needed E = 247.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Schoenfeld, D. A. (1983). Sample-size formula for the proportional-hazards regression model. Biometrics, 39(2), 499-503.
#> 
#> Extensions:
#> - Hsieh, F. Y., & Lavori, P. W. (2000). Sample-size calculations for the Cox proportional hazards regression model with nonbinary covariates. Controlled Clinical Trials, 21(6), 552-560.
#> - Rubinstein, L. V., Gail, M. H., & Santner, T. J. (1981). Planning the duration of a comparative clinical trial with loss to follow-up and a period of continued observation. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 34(9-10), 469-479.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 247 deaths are required. If a separate accrual and follow-up model predicts an event fraction of 60% at analysis, a rough resource estimate is 412 patients. That fraction is an additional assumption, not an output derived from HR by this function.

1.4 Non-Inferiority Trial (Continuous Mean)

  • Population and decision: A randomized parallel trial compares a lower-cost symptom-management strategy with usual care in patients with symptomatic diabetic peripheral neuropathy, while keeping background treatment stable.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Use improvement from baseline to week 12 on a prespecified symptom scale, with larger reductions indicating benefit. Standardize assessment and require sufficient baseline symptoms to avoid a pronounced floor effect.
  • Planning inputs: Assume improvements of 10 and 9.5 points, SD=3, and a maximum acceptable loss of margin = 1 point. Justify the margin using clinical importance and the established comparator effect; it should not be chosen from the anticipated difference alone.
  • Why this design: Demonstrate that study minus control improvement exceeds −1 point. This example uses one-sided α=0.05 and 80% power; a protocol choosing one-sided 0.025 must recalculate accordingly.
  • Formula: \[n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta})\sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2 + \Delta}\right)^2\] Chow et al. (2017), Chapter 4.
res_1_4 <- calculate("rct", "noninferiority", "mean", mean1 = 10, mean2 = 9.5, sd = 3, margin = 1, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_4)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Non-inferiority (means)"
#> • Sample size per group: 50
#> • Total sample size: 100
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = 2*(Z_a+Z_b)^2*sd^2/(mean1-mean2+margin)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta})\sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2 + \Delta}\right)^2$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State non-inferiority hypotheses: H0: mu1 - mu2 <= -margin vs H1: mu1
#> - mu2 > -margin (margin Delta = 1, one-sided alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Effective difference: delta_E = mu1 - mu2 + margin = 10 - 9.50 + 1 =
#> 1.50; SD sigma = 3.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.6449, Z_beta =
#> 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = 2 * (Z_alpha + Z_beta)^2 * sigma^2 /
#> delta_E^2 = 2 * (1.6449 + 0.8416)^2 * 3^2 / (1.50)^2 = 49.46.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 50 per group, total sample size N = 100.
#> Reference:
#> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Chapter 3 (Comparing Means), Section 3.2.2 noninferiority, Eq 3.12, p. 50.
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Eq 11.3, p. 173.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 50 per arm, 100 total. Document the primary analysis population, adherence handling, and missing outcomes alongside the margin justification; they are part of the non-inferiority design.

1.5 Non-Inferiority Trial (Binary Endpoint)

  • Population and decision: An adult lower urinary tract infection trial compares a more convenient study regimen with an effective active comparator, using consistent microbiological and eligibility criteria.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Define clinical cure in a fixed post-treatment visit window, with prespecified rules for rescue treatment, antibiotic switching, and missing visits. Each patient contributes one binary outcome.
  • Planning inputs: Assume both cure rates are 85%, with a maximum acceptable absolute loss of 5 percentage points: p1 = p2 = 0.85, margin = 0.05. The margin is illustrative and requires clinical and effect-preservation justification.
  • Why this design: Use one-sided α=0.05 and 80% power to exclude an unacceptable reduction in cure. A nonsignificant ordinary difference test does not establish non-inferiority.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta})^2\left[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)\right]}{(p_1-p_2+\Delta)^2}\] Chow et al. (2017); Machin et al. (2018) Ch. 11.
res_1_5 <- calculate("rct", "noninferiority", "proportion", p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.85, margin = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_5)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Non-inferiority (proportions)"
#> • Sample size per group: 631
#> • Total sample size: 1262
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p1 = experimental-group response rate
#> • p2 = active-control response rate
#> • margin = non-inferiority margin Delta (one-sided alpha)
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = (Za+Zb)^2 * (p1q1+p2q2) / (p1-p2+margin)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta})^2\left[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)\right]}{(p_1-p_2+\Delta)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State non-inferiority hypotheses: H0: p1 - p2 <= -margin vs H1: p1 -
#> p2 > -margin (margin Delta = 0.05, one-sided alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Effective difference: delta_E = p1 - p2 + margin = 0.85 - 0.85 + 0.05
#> = 0.05.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.6449, Z_beta =
#> 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = (Z_alpha + Z_beta)^2 * [p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)]
#> / delta_E^2 = 630.62.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 631 per group, total sample size N = 1262.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Chapter 4 (Large Sample Tests for Proportions), Section 4.2.2 noninferiority/superiority, Eq 4.8 (p. 78).
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Chapter 11, Eq 11.5-11.6, p. 174.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 631 per arm, 1262 total. If endpoint completeness is expected to be 90%, plan 702 per arm. Treatment failures should not be removed from the denominator as though they were recruitment losses.

1.6 Superiority Trial (Continuous Mean)

  • Population and decision: A knee osteoarthritis trial randomizes patients with sufficient baseline pain to a study topical preparation or active comparator, seeking improvement beyond a prespecified clinically relevant difference.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Measure baseline-to-week-12 reduction on a specified WOMAC pain subscale, with standardized assessments and rules for rescue medication before measurement.
  • Planning inputs: Assume reductions of 12 versus 10 points, SD=3, and margin = 1 point. The effective difference is 12−10−1=1 point; using the full anticipated 2-point difference in the denominator would answer a different question.
  • Why this design: This is superiority beyond a positive margin, with one-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. Specify the scale version, score direction, and clinical reasoning for the margin before observing results.
  • Formula: \[n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta})\sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2 - \Delta}\right)^2\] Chow et al. (2017).
res_1_6 <- calculate("rct", "superiority", "mean", mean1 = 12, mean2 = 10, sd = 3, margin = 1, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_6)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Superiority (means)"
#> • Sample size per group: 112
#> • Total sample size: 224
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = 2*(Z_a+Z_b)^2*sd^2/(mean1-mean2-margin)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta})\sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2 - \Delta}\right)^2$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State superiority hypotheses: H0: mu1 - mu2 <= margin vs H1: mu1 -
#> mu2 > margin (margin Delta = 1, one-sided alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Effective difference: delta_E = mu1 - mu2 - margin = 12 - 10 - 1 = 1;
#> SD sigma = 3.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.6449, Z_beta =
#> 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = 2 * (Z_alpha + Z_beta)^2 * sigma^2 /
#> delta_E^2 = 2 * (1.6449 + 0.8416)^2 * 3^2 / (1)^2 = 111.29.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 112 per group, total sample size N = 224.
#> Reference:
#> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Chapter 3 (Comparing Means), Section 3.2.2 superiority, Eq 3.12, p. 50.
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Eq 11.3, p. 173.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 112 per arm, 224 total. Recruitment must deliver the required primary endpoints; changing the margin after observing outcomes would change the original scientific question.

1.7 Superiority Trial (Binary Endpoint)

  • Population and decision: A dermatology trial compares two oral regimens in patients with confirmed toenail onychomycosis, defining one target nail per patient for the primary analysis.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Evaluate complete cure at a fixed long-term visit, such as week 52, requiring both clinical clearing and mycological negativity. End-of-treatment cosmetic improvement is not the same endpoint.
  • Planning inputs: Assume cure rates of 30% and 20%, and require the difference to exceed 5 percentage points: p1 = 0.30, p2 = 0.20, margin = 0.05. The remaining effective difference is 0.05.
  • Why this design: Use one-sided α=0.05 and 80% power for superiority beyond the margin. Parameter sources should match severity, previous treatment, cure definition, and follow-up duration.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta})^2\left[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)\right]}{(p_1-p_2-\Delta)^2}\] Chow et al. (2017).
res_1_7 <- calculate("rct", "superiority", "proportion", p1 = 0.30, p2 = 0.20, margin = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_7)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Superiority (proportions)"
#> • Sample size per group: 916
#> • Total sample size: 1832
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = (Z_alpha + Z_beta)^2 * (p1*(1-p1) + p2*(1-p2)) / (p1 - p2 - margin)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta})^2[p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)]}{(p_1 - p_2 - \Delta)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State superiority hypotheses: H0: p1 - p2 <= margin vs H1: p1 - p2 >
#> margin (margin Delta = 0.05, one-sided alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Effective difference: delta_E = p1 - p2 - margin = 0.30 - 0.20 - 0.05
#> = 0.05.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.6449, Z_beta =
#> 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = (Z_alpha + Z_beta)^2 * [p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)]
#> / delta_E^2 = (1.6449 + 0.8416)^2 * [0.21 + 0.16] / (0.05)^2 = 915.02.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 916 per group, total sample size N = 1832.
#> Reference:
#> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Chapter 4 (Large Sample Tests for Proportions), Section 4.2.2 noninferiority/ superiority, Eq 4.8 (p. 78).
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Eq 11.5-11.6, p. 174; Fleiss, Tytun & Ury (1980), Biometrics 36(2), 343-346.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 916 per arm, 1832 total. If 10% lack the long-term endpoint, plan 1018 per arm and ensure sufficient follow-up visit capacity.

1.8 Equivalence Trial (Continuous Mean)

  • Population and decision: A parallel randomized study compares two formulations in patients with stable hypothyroidism and stable background dosing, allowing sufficient time for the prespecified steady-state assessment.
  • Procedures and endpoint: This teaching example uses mean steady-state total serum thyroxine, with standardized sampling time and laboratory platform. It illustrates equivalence of a continuous pharmacodynamic endpoint, not a complete bioequivalence or interchangeability assessment.
  • Planning inputs: Assume means of 10 and 10.2 μg/dL, SD=3 μg/dL, and an equivalence corridor of ±1 μg/dL. The SD and margins require endpoint-specific clinical and pilot evidence.
  • Why this design: Both unacceptable directions must be excluded using equivalence testing, with one-sided α=0.05 and target power 80%. Failure to find a difference does not establish equivalence.
  • Formula (TOST): \[n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta/2})\sigma}{\Delta - |\mu_1 - \mu_2|}\right)^2\] Chow et al. (2017).
res_1_8 <- calculate("rct", "equivalence", "mean", mean1 = 10, mean2 = 10.2, sd = 3, margin = 1, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_8)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Equivalence (means)"
#> • Sample size per group: 241
#> • Total sample size: 482
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = 2*(Z_a+Z_b/2)^2*sd^2/(margin-|mean1-mean2|)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta/2})\sigma}{\Delta - |\mu_1 - \mu_2|}\right)^2$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State equivalence hypotheses (TOST): H0: |mu1 - mu2| >= margin vs H1:
#> |mu1 - mu2| < margin (margin Delta = 1, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Margin clearance: Delta - |mu1 - mu2| = 1 - |10 - 10.20| = 0.80; SD
#> sigma = 3.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.6449, Z_(beta/2) =
#> 1.2816.
#> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = 2 * (Z_alpha + Z_(beta/2))^2 * sigma^2 /
#> (Delta - |mu1 - mu2|)^2 = 2 * (1.6449 + 1.2816)^2 * 3^2 / (0.80)^2 = 240.86.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 241 per group, total sample size N = 482.
#> Reference:
#> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Chapter 3 (Comparing Means), Section 3.2.3 equivalence, Eq 3.13, p. 51; the Z_{beta/2} convention is discussed in Section 3.6.1 (p. 67).
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Eq 11.5-11.6, p. 174.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 241 per arm, 482 total. This requirement concerns the single defined continuous endpoint; additional primary or pharmacokinetic outcomes need their own planning.

1.9 Equivalence Trial (Binary Endpoint)

  • Population and decision: An anesthesia service randomizes adults undergoing the same type of surgery to two postoperative analgesic regimens, asking whether a more convenient regimen provides sufficiently similar response rates.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Define success in advance, for example meeting a specified pain-reduction threshold without rescue medication during the first 6 hours. Prespecify rescue use, early withdrawal, and how repeated pain observations form one patient-level result.
  • Planning inputs: Assume response rates of 50% and 52%, with an equivalence corridor of ±10 percentage points: p1 = 0.50, p2 = 0.52, margin = 0.10.
  • Why this design: Use equivalence of independent proportions, one-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. The margin must be justified for this response definition rather than treated as a universal analgesic standard.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta/2})^2\left[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)\right]}{(\Delta-|p_1-p_2|)^2}\] Chow et al. (2017).
res_1_9 <- calculate("rct", "equivalence", "proportion", p1 = 0.50, p2 = 0.52, margin = 0.10, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_1_9)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Equivalence (proportions)"
#> • Sample size per group: 669
#> • Total sample size: 1338
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = (Z_alpha + Z_beta/2)^2 * (p1*(1-p1) + p2*(1-p2)) / (margin - |p1 - p2|)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha} + Z_{\beta/2})^2[p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)]}{(\Delta - |p_1-p_2|)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State equivalence hypotheses (TOST): H0: |p1 - p2| >= margin vs H1:
#> |p1 - p2| < margin (margin Delta = 0.10, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Margin clearance: Delta - |p1 - p2| = 0.10 - |0.50 - 0.52| = 0.08.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.6449, Z_(beta/2) =
#> 1.2816.
#> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = (Z_alpha + Z_(beta/2))^2 * [p1(1-p1) +

#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 669 per group, total sample size N = 1338.
#> Reference:

#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Eq 11.5-11.6, p. 174.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 669 per arm, 1338 total. The count is independent patients with primary outcomes, not the number of repeated pain assessments.

Chapter 2: Paired, Single-Arm, and Crossover Trials

2.1 Paired Means (Pre- vs. Post-Treatment)

  • Population and decision: A rehabilitation clinic follows the same chronic low-back pain patients before and after a 6-week standardized exercise program, using a 0–10 pain scale.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Define improvement as baseline minus week-6 score and use consistent measurement conditions. Each patient’s two scores must be linkable to form one paired difference.
  • Planning inputs: Assume mean improvement meanDiff = 2 points and difference-score SD sdDiff = 3. Estimate the latter from paired pilot data; neither the baseline nor follow-up SD alone is an appropriate substitute.
  • Why this design: Use a two-sided paired-mean calculation with α=0.05 and 80% power. A before–after study estimates change; separating treatment effects from natural history requires an appropriate comparator design.
  • Formula: \[n = \left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma_d}{\mu_d}\right)^2\] Rosner (2015), Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.).
res_2_1 <- calculate("paired", "test", "mean", meanDiff = 2, sdDiff = 3, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_2_1)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Paired means"
#> • Total sample size: 20
#> • Pairs needed: 20
#> • Measurements required: 40
#> • Total individuals: 20
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = ((Z_a/2 + Z_b) * sd_diff / mean_diff)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma_d}{\mu_d}\right)^2$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State paired difference hypotheses: H0: mu_d = 0 vs H1: mu_d != 0
#> (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Expected paired difference mu_d = 2, SD of differences sigma_d = 3.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Normal approximation: n0 = ((Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta) * sigma_d /
#> mu_d)^2 = ((1.96 + 0.8416) * 3 / 2)^2 = 17.66.
#> • Step 5: Exact paired Student's t-test degrees of freedom iteration.
#> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 20 pairs (total individuals = 20).
#> Reference:
#> Rosner, B. (2015). *Fundamentals of biostatistics* (8th ed.). Cengage Learning.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 20 patients must complete both assessments, giving 40 measurements. A pair means two observations from one patient here. With 90% paired completion, recruit 23 patients.

2.2 Paired Binary Outcomes (McNemar / Connor)

  • Population and decision: A chronic-disease clinic introduces a medication reminder program in one cohort and compares adherence success before the program and at week 8.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Apply the same prespecified adherence threshold in both periods. Each patient forms a paired binary record; the question is whether success rises from 60% to 80%, not a comparison of independent cohorts.
  • Planning inputs: Set post-program p1 = 0.80, baseline p2 = 0.60, and discordant proportion psi = 0.25. This implies about 22.5% changing from failure to success and 2.5% changing in the opposite direction; verify that pattern using paired pilot records.
  • Why this design: McNemar/Connor planning uses the discordant pairs, with two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. Both measurements are needed for a complete pair.
  • Formula (Connor): \[n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\psi} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{\psi-\delta^2}\right]^2}{\delta^2}, \quad \delta = |p_1-p_2|\] Connor (1987), Biometrics 43(1), 207-211.
res_2_2 <- calculate("paired", "test", "proportion", p1 = 0.80, p2 = 0.60, psi = 0.25, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_2_2)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Paired binary outcomes (McNemar / Connor)"
#> • Total sample size: 47
#> • Pairs needed: 47
#> • Measurements required: 94
#> • Total individuals: 47
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p1/p2 = expected proportions (or sensitivities) in pairs
#> • psi = expected discordant-pair proportion (pi10 + pi01)
#> • output is in PAIRS of observations; within_subject uses one person per pair,
#> matched_subjects uses two
#> • n_measurements = 2 x pairs; total_individuals counts distinct people
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = [Za*sqrt(psi) + Zb*sqrt(psi-delta^2)]^2/delta^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\psi} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{\psi-\delta^2}\right]^2}{\delta^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Paired binary parameters: p1 = 0.80, p2 = 0.60, discordant pair
#> proportion psi = 0.25, difference delta = |p1 - p2| = 0.20.
#> • Step 2: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 3: Connor formula: n_pairs = [Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt(psi) + Z_beta*sqrt(psi -
#> delta^2)]^2 / delta^2 = 46.63.
#> • Step 4: Round up to integer: Pairs needed = 47.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Connor, R. J. (1987). Sample size for testing differences in proportions for the paired-sample design. Biometrics, 43(1), 207-211.
#> 
#>  Also: Akoglu, H. (2022). Turkish Journal of Emergency Medicine, 22(4), Table 2 Eq 3b + Tables 6A/6B (uncorrected and Yates-corrected values).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 47 patients with complete pairs, or 94 assessments. At 90% paired completion, recruit 53 patients; doubling the observations does not double the number of distinct people.

2.3 Single-Arm Mean vs. Historical Benchmark

  • Population and decision: A rare-disease rehabilitation project evaluates exercise endurance after a training program, using a comparable historical mean as a fixed benchmark because recruitment is limited.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Measure fully observed endurance duration in a standardized constant-load exercise test at week 8, in minutes. This is a continuous functional endpoint, not a censored survival time; historical and new cohorts need comparable severity, workloads, and stopping rules.
  • Planning inputs: Treat the historical mean as mu0 = 10 minutes, anticipate mu1 = 12, and assume sigma = 3, with two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power.
  • Why this design: This approximation treats the reference mean as known without error. A small or poorly matched historical sample requires a design that incorporates its uncertainty rather than treating a survival median as a known mean.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2 \sigma^2}{(\mu_1 - \mu_0)^2}\] Machin et al. (2018), Chapter 5.
res_2_3 <- calculate("rctSingleArm", "test", "mean", mu0 = 10, mu1 = 12, sigma = 3, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_2_3)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Single-arm trial (continuous, vs fixed value)"
#> • Required sample size: 18
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • mu0 = reference/historical control mean (the null value)
#> • mu1 = anticipated treatment mean
#> • sigma = population standard deviation
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = (Za/2 + Zb)^2 * sigma^2 / (mu1-mu0)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2 \sigma^2}{(\mu_1 - \mu_0)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Single-arm continuous hypotheses: H0: mu = 10 vs H1: mu = 12, SD
#> sigma = 3 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Effect size delta = |mu1 - mu0| = |12 - 10| = 2.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Sample size: n = (Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta)^2 * sigma^2 / delta^2 = (1.96
#> + 0.8416)^2 * 3^2 / (2)^2 = 17.66.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Required sample size n = 18.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Machin, D., Campbell, M. J., Tan, S. B., & Tan, S. H. (2018). Sample Sizes for Clinical, Laboratory and Epidemiology Studies (4th ed.). Wiley. Chapter 5 (Continuous Outcomes, single-sample comparison).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 18 patients with the defined endpoint. If 10% cannot complete the exercise assessment, plan 20 recruits; comparability of the reference remains central to interpretation.

2.4 Single-Arm Proportion vs. Historical Benchmark

  • Population and decision: An exploratory single-arm study enrolls relapsed/refractory lymphoma patients with defined prior treatment lines, comparing a new protocol with a fixed historical response rate.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Assess objective response at day 90 using consistent criteria. Prespecify deaths before assessment, rescue treatment, and unevaluable patients; restricting the denominator to surviving imaged patients changes the endpoint.
  • Planning inputs: Use teaching assumptions p0 = 0.70 and p1 = 0.80. Actual evidence must match treatment line, response definition, and assessment window to avoid an inappropriate historical comparator.
  • Why this design: This example uses a two-sided normal approximation with α=0.05 and 80% power. For an exact one-sided success cutoff or interim futility decision, consider the following A’Hern or Simon examples.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_0)^2}\] Hajian-Tilaki (2014), Eq 6.8.
res_2_4 <- calculate("rctSingleArm", "test", "proportion", p0 = 0.70, p1 = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_2_4)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Single-arm trial (binary, vs fixed value)"
#> • Required sample size: 153
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p0 = null/historical control proportion
#> • p1 = anticipated treatment proportion
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = [Za*sqrt(p0q0) + Zb*sqrt(p1q1)]^2/(p1-p0)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)}\right]^2}{(p_1 - p_0)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Single-arm binary hypotheses: H0: p = 0.70 vs H1: p = 0.80 (alpha =
#> 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 3: Sample size: n = [Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt(p0*q0) + Z_beta*sqrt(p1*q1)]^2 /
#> (p1 - p0)^2 = 152.48.
#> • Step 4: Round up to integer: Required sample size n = 153.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. Journal of Biomedical Informatics, 48, 193-204 (Eq 6.8; worked example 0.70 vs 0.80 -> n=153).
#> 
#>  Also: Akoglu, H. (2022). Table 2, Equation 2; Machin et al. (2018) Ch.3.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 153 patients with ascertainable primary outcomes. This count addresses the planned distinction between 70% and 80%; it does not promise that the eventual response rate will equal the alternative.

2.5 Phase II Simon’s Optimal Two-Stage Design

  • Population and decision: A single-arm phase-II sarcoma study enrolls patients with measurable advanced disease and consistent previous treatment eligibility, seeking early termination when the regimen has inadequate activity.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Confirm objective response at approximately 8 weeks using prespecified criteria. Allow stage-1 patients to reach the assessment window and verify their outcomes before the formal continuation decision.
  • Planning inputs: Set an unacceptable response rate p0 = 0.10, a promising rate p1 = 0.30, one-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. Both rates must refer to the same disease subgroup and response definition.
  • Why this design: optimizer = "optimal" minimizes expected enrollment under the null, potentially accepting a larger maximum total than the minimax design.
  • Formula: exact binomial enumeration (Simon 1989). The design \((r_1/n_1, r/n)\) satisfies \[P_p(\text{reject }H_0) = \sum_{x_1=r_1+1}^{n_1}\binom{n_1}{x_1}p^{x_1}(1-p)^{n_1-x_1}\,P_p(X_2 > r-x_1), \quad P_{p_0}(\text{reject }H_0)\le\alpha\] and the analogous expression under \(p_1\) must reach the target power. Simon (1989), Controlled Clinical Trials 10(1), 1-10.
res_2_5 <- calculate("singleArmPhaseII", "test", "proportion", p0 = 0.10, p1 = 0.30, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8, optimizer = "optimal")
print(res_2_5)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Single-arm phase II (Simon two-stage, optimal)"
#> • Stage 1 sample size: 10
#> • Stage 1 futility boundary (stop if responses <= r1): 1
#> • Total sample size (both stages): 29
#> • Overall boundary (declare effective if responses > r): 5
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p0 = unacceptable response rate (null)
#> • p1 = desirable response rate (alternative)
#> • stage 1: stop for futility if responses <= r_stage_1 of n_stage_1
#> • overall: declare effective if responses > r_total of n_total
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `exact binomial: P(effective|p0) <= alpha and P(effective|p1) >= power`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid p_0) \le \alpha \quad \text{and} \quad P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid p_1) \ge 1-\beta$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State phase II hypotheses: H0: p <= 0.10 (unacceptable) vs H1: p >=
#> 0.30 (promising) (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Exhaustive exact binomial search under 'optimal' criterion.
#> • Step 3: Stage 1: Accrue n1 = 10 patients; stop early for futility if
#> responses <= r1 = 1.
#> • Step 4: Stage 2: If > 1 responses observed, accrue additional 19 patients up
#> to total n = 29.
#> • Step 5: Final decision: Declare effective if total responses > r = 5
#> (Expected sample size under H0 = 15).
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Simon, R. (1989). Optimal two-stage designs for phase II clinical trials. Controlled Clinical Trials, 10(1), 1-10.
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Chapter 17 (Therapeutic Exploratory Trials).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and stopping rules: Enroll 10 initially and stop for futility if responses are ≤1. Otherwise add 19 patients to a maximum of 29. Reject the null only if total responses exceed 5 (at least 6). Stage 1 is included in the maximum total.

2.6 Phase II Simon’s Minimax Two-Stage Design

  • Population and decision: A center addresses the same advanced sarcoma response question but has a firm ceiling on drug supply and eligible patients, making the worst-case enrollment especially important.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Use the same response definition and assessment window, with a prespecified stage-wise continuation rule. Do not switch optimization criteria after examining interim responses.
  • Planning inputs: Keep p0 = 0.10, p1 = 0.30, α=0.05, and 80% power, changing only optimizer = "minimax" so resource comparisons use the same error constraints.
  • Why this design: Minimax minimizes the maximum total sample size, not necessarily the expected number under the null. Compare both criteria when budgeting assessments and medication.
res_2_6 <- calculate("singleArmPhaseII", "test", "proportion", p0 = 0.10, p1 = 0.30, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8, optimizer = "minimax")
print(res_2_6)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Single-arm phase II (Simon two-stage, minimax)"
#> • Stage 1 sample size: 15
#> • Stage 1 futility boundary (stop if responses <= r1): 1
#> • Total sample size (both stages): 25
#> • Overall boundary (declare effective if responses > r): 5
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p0 = unacceptable response rate (null)
#> • p1 = desirable response rate (alternative)
#> • stage 1: stop for futility if responses <= r_stage_1 of n_stage_1
#> • overall: declare effective if responses > r_total of n_total
#> ! Multiple designs may achieve the minimum total sample size N;
#> ! this implementation selects the design minimizing Type I error (alpha) among ties.
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `exact binomial: P(effective|p0) <= alpha and P(effective|p1) >= power`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid p_0) \le \alpha \quad \text{and} \quad P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid p_1) \ge 1-\beta$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State phase II hypotheses: H0: p <= 0.10 (unacceptable) vs H1: p >=
#> 0.30 (promising) (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Exhaustive exact binomial search under 'minimax' criterion.
#> • Step 3: Stage 1: Accrue n1 = 15 patients; stop early for futility if
#> responses <= r1 = 1.
#> • Step 4: Stage 2: If > 1 responses observed, accrue additional 10 patients up
#> to total n = 25.
#> • Step 5: Final decision: Declare effective if total responses > r = 5
#> (Expected sample size under H0 = 19.50).
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Simon, R. (1989). Optimal two-stage designs for phase II clinical trials. Controlled Clinical Trials, 10(1), 1-10.
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Chapter 17 (Therapeutic Exploratory Trials).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and stopping rules: Stage 1 enrolls 15, stopping if responses are ≤1; the maximum total is 25, with rejection requiring more than 5 responses. Compare that maximum with the optimal design’s 29 patients.

2.7 A’Hern Exact Single-Stage Binomial Design

  • Population and decision: Another center studies the same sarcoma response question, but recruitment is concentrated and endpoint assessment delayed, so an interim futility analysis would not meaningfully affect enrollment.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Perform one formal decision after every enrolled patient reaches the prespecified objective-response assessment window, retaining comparability with the historical benchmark.
  • Planning inputs: Set p0 = 0.10, p1 = 0.30, one-sided α=0.05, and 80% power, then search the exact binomial distribution for a feasible total and rejection boundary.
  • Why this design: A’Hern is a single-stage design. In this implementation, r_total is the boundary that must be exceeded, not the minimum number of successes itself.
res_2_7 <- SampleSizeCalc:::calculate_ahern(p0 = 0.10, p1 = 0.30, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_2_7)

#> [1] "p0 = unacceptable response rate"

  • Result and decision rule: Enroll 25; at least 6 responses are needed. The rule is X > r_total, whereas some publications use a symbol for the minimum success count.
  • Formula: exact binomial — \(P(X > r \mid p_0) \le \alpha\) and \(P(X > r \mid p_1) \ge 1-\beta\) (A’Hern 2001).

2.8 2x2 Crossover Trial (Continuous Mean)

  • Population and decision: A respiratory clinic compares two short-acting inhaled formulations in stable asthma patients able to complete repeat lung-function testing, randomizing the order to AB or BA.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Each patient receives one formulation in each period, with FEV1 percent predicted measured at a fixed post-dose time. Prespecify washout based on duration of action and control background therapy and testing conditions.
  • Planning inputs: Target delta = 2 percentage points with within-subject period-error SD sigma_within = 3. This is not the same quantity as the SD of the difference between two observations.
  • Why this design: Use a 2×2 crossover calculation with two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. Stability and negligible carryover support the design, and the two sequences need balanced recruitment.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{2(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2\sigma_w^2}{\delta^2}\] Senn (2002), Cross-over Trials in Clinical Research (2nd ed.).
res_2_8 <- calculate("crossover", "test", "mean", delta = 2, sigma_within = 3, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_2_8)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "2x2 crossover trial (continuous)"
#> • Required sample size: 18
#> • Total sample size: 36
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • delta = anticipated treatment difference (mu_T - mu_R)
#> • sigma_within = within-subject standard deviation
#> • n_required/n_per_sequence = subjects per sequence; total_n = 2 x that
#> ! This is the normal-approximation form (Julious 2004 Eq 6.6; Machin Eq 11.4). Senn (2002) Section 9.5.1, Eq 9.18-9.20, refines it with a Student t correction (df = n - 2), which typically needs 1-2 extra subjects; use the returned total as a lower bound and add 2 for exact 80% power.
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n_total = 2 (Za/2 + Zb)^2 sigma_w^2 / delta^2 ; n_per_sequence = n_total/2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n_{\text{total}} = \frac{2(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2\sigma_w^2}{\delta^2}, \quad n_{\text{sequence}} = \frac{n_{\text{total}}}{2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: 2x2 crossover trial (continuous).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: delta = 2, sigma_within = 3, alpha = 0.05, power =
#> 0.80.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: n_total = 2 (Za/2 + Zb)^2 sigma_w^2 / delta^2 ;
#> n_per_sequence = n_total/2.
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Required sample size: 18; Total
#> sample size: 36.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Senn, S. (2002). Cross-over Trials in Clinical Research (2nd ed.). Wiley. Section 9.5 'Sample-size issues', Eq 9.18-9.20, pp. 278-280 (sigma^2 = 2 sigma_w^2 for a basic estimator, Var = sigma^2/n, df = n - 2, n = total patients with n/2 per sequence).
#> 
#>  Also: Julious, S. A. (2004). Tutorial in biostatistics: sample sizes for clinical trials with normal data. Statistics in Medicine, 23(12), 1921-1986 (Section 6.3 'Cross-over trials', Eq 6.3/6.6; n there is the total sample size, and the reported quantity is per sequence).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: The function returns 18 per sequence, 36 patients total, each completing two periods. With 10% incomplete follow-up, plan 20 per sequence; period measurements are not additional independent patients.

2.9 Bioequivalence (BE) Exact TOST

  • Population and decision: A randomized two-sequence, two-period pharmacokinetic study compares test and reference formulations in eligible healthy adults, each receiving both formulations in the assigned order.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Evaluate a single specified log-transformed PK parameter, such as AUC, using fixed sampling, washout, assay, and evaluable-profile rules.
  • Planning inputs: Assume within-subject cv = 0.25, expected geometric mean ratio theta0 = 1.0, bounds 0.80–1.25, one-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. Source the CV from compatible crossover data for that PK parameter.
  • Why this design: The function evaluates log-scale TOST power and searches sequence size. If AUC, Cmax, or other co-primary PK endpoints must all pass, assess each requirement and choose a study size that covers the prespecified objectives.
  • Formula (exact noncentral \(t\), Phillips 1990): \[\text{Power} = F_t(-t_{1-\alpha, \nu}; \nu, \delta_2) - F_t(t_{1-\alpha, \nu}; \nu, \delta_1), \quad \nu = N-2\] 
res_2_9 <- calculate("bioequivalence", cv = 0.25, theta0 = 1.0, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_2_9)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Bioequivalence (2x2 crossover, exact TOST integration)"
#> • Required sample size: 12
#> • Total sample size: 24
#> • Power achieved: 0.8372
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • cv = intra-subject coefficient of variation (log scale implied)
#> • theta0 = anticipated geometric mean ratio (true ratio, default 1.0)
#> • margin = [0.80, 1.25] average BE criteria
#> • n is per sequence; total subjects = 2n
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `power = E[max(0, Phi((U-mu)/SE-t*sqrt(V/df))-Phi((L-mu)/SE+t*sqrt(V/df)))], V
#> ~ chi-square(df), df=N-2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$\mathrm{Power}=E\!\left[\max\!\left\{0,\Phi\!\left(\frac{U-\mu}{SE}-t\sqrt{V/\nu}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{L-\mu}{SE}+t\sqrt{V/\nu}\right)\right\}\right],\quad V\sim\chi^2_\nu,\ \nu=N-2$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Log-scale within-subject SD = sqrt(log(1+CV^2)) = 0.246221;
#> anticipated log ratio = 0.000000.
#> • Step 2: TOST log limits are [-0.223144, 0.223144], each with one-sided alpha
#> 0.0500.
#> • Step 3: Integrate the conditional normal acceptance probability over the
#> chi-square variance estimate (df = N-2); negative-width acceptance intervals
#> contribute zero.
#> • Step 4: Search balanced even totals for the smallest N meeting the target
#> power.
#> • Step 5: n = 12 per sequence, total N = 24, achieved power = 0.837226 (target
#> 0.8000).
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Phillips, K. F. (1990). Power of the two one-sided tests procedure in bioequivalence. Journal of Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics, 18(2), 137-144.
#> 
#>  Also: Julious, S. A. (2004). Tutorial in biostatistics: sample sizes for clinical trials with normal data. Statistics in Medicine, 23(12), 1921-1986 (Section 6.3 'Cross-over trials', Eq 6.1-6.9; the non-central t power expression is Eq 6.8).
#>  Schuirmann, D. J. (1987). J Pharmacokinet Biopharm, 15(6), 657-680;
#>  Chow & Liu (2009). Design and Analysis of Bioavailability and Bioequivalence Studies.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 12 per sequence, 24 complete subjects, with calculated power 83.72%. With 10% incomplete profiles, plan 28 recruits across balanced sequences. Recalculate if the expected ratio departs from 1.0.

Chapter 3: Observational and Epidemiological Studies

3.1 Prospective Cohort Study (Cumulative Incidence & RR)

  • Population and decision: A cardiovascular cohort enrolls adults free of coronary disease at baseline but at appreciable cardiovascular risk, defining current smokers and never-smokers before a planned 5-year follow-up.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Use annual contacts and record verification to identify the first prespecified coronary event, with consistent ascertainment in both exposure groups. Existing cases do not enter an incidence denominator.
  • Planning inputs: Assume 5-year risks of 20% and 30%, ratio = 1, and dropout = 0.10. These are cumulative risks over a fixed period, not cross-sectional prevalence or annual incidence densities.
  • Why this design: A two-proportion approximation plans detection of the risk difference with two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. Exposure is not randomized; confounding control and multivariable event requirements need separate analysis planning.
  • Formula: \[n_{1} = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{(1+\frac{1}{m})\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)+\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{m}}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_0)^2}, \quad n = \frac{n_1}{1-d}\] Bhardwaj et al. (2024), J Family Med Prim Care 13(7), 2559.
res_3_1 <- calculate("cohort", "test", "proportion", p0 = 0.20, p1 = 0.30, ratio = 1, dropout = 0.10, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_3_1)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Cohort study (cumulative incidence, RR)"
#> • Sample size per group: 327
#> • Exposed group: 327
#> • Unexposed group: 327
#> • Total sample size: 654
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p0 = unexposed-group cumulative incidence
#> • p1 = exposed-group cumulative incidence
#> • ratio = unexposed:exposed allocation (m)
#> • effect measure: risk ratio RR (estimable in cohort designs)
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n1 = [Za*sqrt((1+1/m)*pbar*(1-pbar)) + Zb*sqrt(p1q1+p0q0/m)]^2/(p1-p0)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n_{1} = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{(1+\frac{1}{m})\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)+\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{m}}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_0)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Specify proportions: unexposed p0 = 0.20, exposed p1 = 0.30,
#> allocation ratio m = 1 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Weighted average proportion: p_bar = (p1 + m*p0) / (1 + m) = 0.25.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Calculate exposed sample size: n_exposed =
#> [Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt((1+1/m)*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_beta*sqrt(p1*q1 + p0*q0/m)]^2 /
#> (p1 - p0)^2 = 293.15.
#> • Step 5: Calculate unexposed sample size: n_unexposed = m * n_exposed = 1 *
#> 293.15 = 293.15.
#> • Step 6: Round up before dropout inflation: ceiling(n_exposed) = 294,
#> ceiling(m*n_exposed) = 294; apply dropout d = 0.10 using ceiling(n/(1-d)).
#> Exposed = 327, Unexposed = 327, Total sample size N = 654.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Bhardwaj et al. (2024). Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care, 13(7), 2559 (worked example: p0=0.20, p1=0.30, m=1 -> 293/group).
#> 
#>  Also: Schlesselman, J. J. (1982). Case-Control Studies. Oxford University Press (cohort/case-control shared formula, roles swapped); Machin et al. (2018) Ch.3.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 327 per group, 654 total, already including the specified 10% loss adjustment. Do not apply the same inflation again, and budget maintenance of the cohort over the full 5 years.

3.2 Cohort Study (Person-Time Incidence Rate Ratio)

  • Population and decision: An occupational cohort compares respiratory-disease incidence densities between exposed and unexposed workers whose entry and exit times vary, requiring observed person-time as the denominator.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Define first incident disease and time at risk consistently, recording events and censoring. This Poisson rate approximation assumes approximately stable group-specific rates during observation.
  • Planning inputs: Assume rate1 = 0.20 and rate0 = 0.10 events per person-year with equal person-time allocation. Convert sources reported per thousand person-years to the same units before calculation.
  • Why this design: The result is required person-time, with two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. Convert to workers using the realistic average observable time at risk, accounting for events and losses.
  • Formula: \[T_{0} = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2(\lambda_1/r+\lambda_0)}{(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)^2}, \quad T_1 = r \cdot T_0\] Machin et al. (2018), Chapter 6.
res_3_2 <- calculate("cohort", "test", "rate", rate0 = 0.10, rate1 = 0.20, ratio = 1, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_3_2)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Cohort study (incidence rate ratio, person-time)"
#> • Person-time, exposed group: 236
#> • Person-time, unexposed group: 236
#> • Expected events: 71
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • rate0 = unexposed-group incidence rate (events per person-time)
#> • rate1 = exposed-group incidence rate
#> • ratio = exposed:unexposed person-time ratio (r >= 1)
#> • effect measure: incidence rate ratio IRR
#> • person-time = total follow-up time; for fixed duration FT, subjects needed =
#> person-time / FT
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `T0 = (Za/2+Zb)^2 * (l1/r + l0) / (l1-l0)^2 ; T1 = r*T0`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$T_{0} = \frac{(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2(\lambda_1/r+\lambda_0)}{(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)^2}, \quad T_1 = r \cdot T_0$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Specify incidence rates: unexposed lambda0 = 0.10, exposed lambda1 =
#> 0.20, person-time ratio r = 1.
#> • Step 2: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 3: Calculate required person-time for unexposed group: T0 = (Z_(alpha/2)
#> + Z_beta)^2 * (lambda1/r + lambda0) / (lambda1 - lambda0)^2 = 235.47.
#> • Step 4: Calculate required person-time for exposed group: T1 = r * T0 = 1 *
#> 235.47 = 235.47.
#> • Step 5: Expected events: E = lambda0 * T0 + lambda1 * T1 = 71.
#> • Step 6: Round up to integer: Person-time unexposed = 236, Person-time exposed
#> = 236.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Machin, D., Campbell, M. J., Tan, S. B., & Tan, S. H. (2018). Sample Sizes for Clinical, Laboratory and Epidemiology Studies (4th ed.). Wiley. Chapter 6 (Rate Outcomes).
#> 
#>  Also: Breslow, N. E., & Day, N. E. (1987). Statistical Methods in Cancer Research Vol. II. IARC (person-time rate comparison).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 236 unexposed and 236 exposed person-years, with about 71 expected events. If each worker contributes an average of 2 observed years at risk, rough group sizes are 118 and 118 workers.

3.3 Case-Control Study (Odds Ratio)

  • Population and decision: A hospital-linked community registry studies long-term night work and first myocardial infarction, enrolling incident cases and controls from the same source population that could have produced those cases.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Measure night-work exposure in a fixed window before the case’s index date using records or a standardized questionnaire; use comparable index windows for controls to avoid treating post-infarction work changes as prior exposure.
  • Planning inputs: Assume 30% of controls were exposed, target OR = 2.0, and use one control per case: p0 = 0.30, m = 1. Here p0 is control exposure prevalence, not disease prevalence.
  • Why this design: This is an unmatched case-control comparison. A 1:1 group ratio does not mean individual age matching; the next example addresses matched pairs.
  • Formula (Schlesselman): \[n_{cases} = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{(1+1/m)\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1) + p_0(1-p_0)/m}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_0)^2}\] Schlesselman (1982), Case-Control Studies, Oxford University Press.
res_3_3 <- calculate("caseControl", p0 = 0.30, OR = 2.0, m = 1, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_3_3)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Case-control"
#> • Cases needed: 141
#> • Controls needed: 141
#> • Total subjects: 282
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n_cases = [Z_alpha/2 * sqrt((1+1/m)*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_beta * sqrt(p1*(1-p1)
#> + p0*(1-p0)/m)]^2 / (p1 - p0)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n_{cases} = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{(1+1/m)\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1) + p_0(1-p_0)/m}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_0)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Compute case exposure rate from Odds Ratio: p1 = (OR * p0) / (1 - p0
#> + OR * p0) = (2 * 0.30) / (1 - 0.30 + 2 * 0.30) = 0.4615.
#> • Step 2: Weighted average exposure (matching ratio m = 1): p_bar = (p1 + m*p0)
#> / (1 + m) = 0.3808.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Schlesselman formula for cases: n_cases =
#> [Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt((1+1/m)*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Z_beta*sqrt(p1*(1-p1) +
#> p0*(1-p0)/m)]^2 / (p1 - p0)^2 = 140.66.
#> • Step 5: Calculate controls needed: n_controls = m * n_cases = 1 * 140.66 =
#> 140.66.
#> • Step 6: Round up to integer: Cases needed = 141, Controls needed = 141, Total
#> subjects = 282.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Schlesselman, J. J. (1982). Case-control studies: Design, conduct, analysis. Oxford University Press.
#> 
#> IARC classic: Breslow, N. E., & Day, N. E. (1980). Statistical methods in cancer research: Volume I - The analysis of case-control studies. IARC Scientific Publications No. 32.
#> 
#> For individually matched designs (not the formula implemented here): Dupont, W. D. (1988). Power calculations for matched case-control studies. Biometrics, 44(4), 1157-1168; see the caseControlMatched design.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 141 cases and 141 controls, 282 people total. Assess case availability and control participation separately; additional controls do not automatically compensate for too few cases.

3.4 1:1 Matched Case-Control Study

  • Population and decision: A study of oral contraceptive use and first ischemic stroke in young women pairs each incident case with an age-comparable control from the same source population.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Measure exposure for both women before the same index date and preserve the pairing in analysis. Discordant pairs, where only one member was exposed, provide the main information.
  • Planning inputs: Given control exposure 30% and OR = 2, the function derives case exposure and discordance using an independence-within-pair approximation. Real matching can induce exposure correlation, so verify the approximation using matched pilot tables.
  • Why this design: Use a 1:1 matched case-control calculation with two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. A pair here consists of two people, unlike a patient’s before–after observations.
  • Formula (Dupont discordant-pairs): \[n_{pairs} = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\psi} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{\psi-\delta^2}\right]^2}{\delta^2}, \quad \psi = p_1(1-p_0)+p_0(1-p_1)\] Dupont (1988), Biometrics 44(4), 1157-1168.
res_3_4 <- calculate("caseControlMatched", p0 = 0.30, OR = 2.0, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_3_4)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Individually matched case-control (1:1)"
#> • Total sample size: 288
#> • Cases needed: 144
#> • Controls needed: 144
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p0 = control-group exposure rate
#> • OR = odds ratio to detect (p1 derived from p0 and OR)
#> • psi = expected discordant-pair proportion (pi10 + pi01 = p1*(1-p0) +
#> p0*(1-p1))
#> • note = individually matched designs require discordant-pair proportions
#> (psi), NOT the discordant odds ratio
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = [Za*sqrt(psi) + Zb*sqrt(psi-delta^2)]^2/delta^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n_{pairs} = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\psi} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{\psi-\delta^2}\right]^2}{\delta^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Matched case-control parameters: control exposure p0 = 0.30, Odds
#> Ratio OR = 2 (alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Case exposure rate: p1 = (OR * p0) / (1 - p0 + OR * p0) = 0.4615.
#> • Step 3: Discordant pair probability: psi = pi10 + pi01 = 0.4846; difference
#> delta = |pi10 - pi01| = 0.1615.
#> • Step 4: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 5: Apply Dupont/Connor formula: n_pairs = [Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt(psi) +
#> Z_beta*sqrt(psi - delta^2)]^2 / delta^2 = 143.38.
#> • Step 6: Round up to integer: Pairs needed = 144 (Cases = 144, Controls =
#> 144).
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Dupont, W. D. (1988). Power calculations for matched case-control studies. Biometrics, 44(4), 1157-1168.
#> 
#>  Also: Schlesselman, J. J. (1982). Case-Control Studies, Oxford University Press (matched-pair approximation, p.174); Connor, R. J. (1987). Biometrics, 43(1), 207-211.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 144 complete matched pairs, 288 people. With 90% complete-pair retention, prepare 160 pairs and plan verification and analysis at the pair level.

3.5 Cross-Sectional Association Survey

  • Population and decision: A community survey compares current hypertension prevalence in obese and non-obese adults drawn from the same sampling frame, measuring exposure and outcome at the same survey visit.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Prespecify BMI groups and hypertension ascertainment, using consistent BP measurement and medication-history collection. The endpoint is existing disease, not future incidence.
  • Planning inputs: Assume non-obese p0 = 0.20 and obese p1 = 0.30, equal comparison groups, two-sided α=0.05, and 80% power.
  • Why this design: This calculation serves an association comparison. Exposure quotas affect estimation of overall prevalence, and village or household cluster sampling requires its own design-effect consideration.
  • Formula: same two-proportion kernel as 3.1 with \(m = 1\) (Machin et al. 2018, Ch. 3).
res_3_5 <- calculate("crosstab", p0 = 0.20, p1 = 0.30, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_3_5)
