  • Result and recruitment: 294 per group, 588 total. If only 20% of screened residents are obese, obtaining that group’s quota requires roughly 1470 screened residents on average, exceeding the final comparison sample.

Chapter 4: Single-Sample Precision Estimation

4.1 Single Proportion Estimation (Prevalence Survey)

  • Population and decision: A county health service estimates diabetes prevalence in a defined adult age range using an explicit population register, initially planning for independently sampled individuals.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Classify each participant using a consistent diagnostic-history and laboratory protocol, with prespecified age eligibility and nonresponse handling across communities.
  • Planning inputs: Assume p = 0.10 and a 95% CI absolute half-width precision = 0.02. Two percentage points of absolute error differs from 20% relative error, even though they coincide numerically at this assumed prevalence.
  • Why this design: This is precision estimation, requiring neither a between-group effect nor power. Account separately for cluster sampling, finite population correction when relevant, and nonresponse.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{d^2}\] Lwanga & Lemeshow (1991), WHO; Bhardwaj et al. (2024), p. 2558.
res_4_1 <- calculate("singleProportion", p = 0.10, precision = 0.02, alpha = 0.05)
print(res_4_1)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Single proportion estimation (precision)"
#> • Required sample size: 865
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p = expected proportion (e.g. prevalence)
#> • precision = margin of error d (half-width of the CI)
#> • confidence level = 95%
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = Z^2 * p(1-p) / d^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{d^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Specify anticipated proportion p = 0.10, margin of error d = 0.02
#> (absolute precision), alpha = 0.05.
#> • Step 2: Determine critical value: Z_(1-alpha/2) = 1.96 (confidence level =
#> 95%).
#> • Step 3: Compute variance component: p * (1 - p) = 0.10 * 0.90 = 0.09.
#> • Step 4: Calculate unrounded sample size: n = Z_(1-alpha/2)^2 * p * (1 - p) /
#> d^2 = (1.96)^2 * 0.09 / (0.02)^2 = 864.33.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Required sample size n = 865.
#> Reference:
#> Bhardwaj et al. (2024). Determination of sample size for various study designs in medical research: A practical primer. Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care, 13(7), 2555-2561 (p. 2558).
#> 
#> Also: Lwanga, S. K., & Lemeshow, S. (1991). Sample size determination in health studies: A practical manual. World Health Organization.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 865 valid disease-status records. At 90% response, invite about 962 people; any design-effect adjustment must also be incorporated into the actual sampling plan.

4.2 Single Mean Estimation

  • Population and decision: A pediatric service estimates mean serum ferritin in a specific healthy-child age stratum, with eligibility addressing factors such as acute infection that can alter ferritin.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Obtain one measurement per child using standardized collection and assays. The objective is a population mean and its CI, not a reference interval covering 95% of individual children.
  • Planning inputs: Assume sigma = 10 μg/L, absolute half-width precision = 2 μg/L, and 95% confidence. If analysis changes to a log scale, both SD and precision must be specified on that scale.
  • Why this design: Use single-mean precision planning and inspect pilot distributions and outlier handling. This sample size does not establish precision for reference-interval endpoints.
  • Formula: \[n = \left(\frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{d}\right)^2\] Machin et al. (2018), Ch. 9.
res_4_2 <- calculate("singleMean", sigma = 10, precision = 2, alpha = 0.05)
print(res_4_2)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Single mean estimation (precision)"
#> • Required sample size: 99
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • sigma = population standard deviation (from pilot/literature)
#> • precision = margin of error d
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `smallest integer n >= 2 with t_(n-1, 1-a/2) * sigma / sqrt(n) <= d`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \min\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}: k\ge 2,\ \frac{t_{k-1,1-\alpha/2}\sigma}{\sqrt{k}}\le d\right\}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Plan mean precision with sigma = 10, CI half-width d = 2, alpha =
#> 0.05.
#> • Step 2: Normal approximation starting size is 96.04; require at least two
#> observations for a t interval.
#> • Step 3: Search integers for the smallest n satisfying
#> t_(n-1,1-alpha/2)*sigma/sqrt(n) <= d.
#> • Step 4: n = 99, df = 98, t critical value = 1.984467, achieved half-width =
#> 1.994465 <= 2.000000.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Machin, D., Campbell, M. J., Tan, S. B., & Tan, S. H. (2018). Sample Sizes for Clinical, Laboratory and Epidemiology Studies (4th ed.). Wiley. Chapter 9 (Confidence Intervals), Eq 9.18, p. 152 (iterative Student t form; Eq 9.19 for relative precision).
#> 
#>  Also: Bhardwaj et al. (2024), p. 2558 (continuous outcome precision, normal approximation).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 99 valid measurements. With 5% unusable specimens, prepare 105 children; estimating separate age or sex strata requires separate stratum-level planning.

4.3 Pearson Correlation Coefficient Precision (Fisher-z)

  • Population and decision: A nutrition study estimates the Pearson correlation between waist circumference and DXA body-fat percentage in adults with a representative range of body sizes, avoiding selection solely from extremes.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Obtain both measurements on the same day and prespecify how replicate waist measurements are averaged. Each participant supplies one complete pair of continuous values.
  • Planning inputs: Assume r=0.50 and a 95% CI half-width of approximately 0.10, corresponding to total width about 0.20. The correlation is not R² and is not a measure of interchangeability.
  • Why this design: Use Fisher-z precision planning for correlation. Demonstrating that two measurements can substitute for each other requires separate agreement objectives and methods.
  • Formula (Machin Eqs 19.5-19.8): \[N_{P0} = \frac{4 z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 (1-r^2)^2}{w^2} + 3, \quad N_{Final} = (N_{P0}-3)\left(\frac{w_0}{w}\right)^2 + 3\] Machin et al. (2018), Ch. 19, pp. 307-308 (matches presize::prec_cor).
res_4_3 <- calculate("singleCorrelation", r = 0.50, precision = 0.10, alpha = 0.05)
print(res_4_3)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Single correlation estimation (Fisher z precision)"
#> • Required sample size: 219
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • r = anticipated correlation coefficient
#> • precision = margin of error d (CI half-width, w = 2*d)
#> • confidence level = 95%
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `Machin 19.5-19.8: N_P0 = 4*z^2*(1-r^2)^2/w^2 + 3, refined via Fisher z bounds`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$N_{P0} = \frac{4 z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 (1-r^2)^2}{w^2} + 3, \quad N_{Final} = (N_{P0}-3)\left(\frac{w_0}{w}\right)^2 + 3$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Specify anticipated correlation r = 0.50, CI half-width d = 0.10
#> (width w = 2d = 0.20), alpha = 0.05.
#> • Step 2: Determine critical value: Z_(1-alpha/2) = 1.96.
#> • Step 3: Machin initial estimate: N_P0 = 4 * Z^2 * (1 - r^2)^2 / w^2 + 3 =
#> 219.08.
#> • Step 4: Refine via Fisher z transformation limits to adjust for confidence
#> interval skewness.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Required sample size n = 219.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Machin, D., Campbell, M. J., Tan, S. B., & Tan, S. H. (2018). Sample Sizes for Clinical, Laboratory and Epidemiology Studies (4th ed.). Wiley. Chapter 19 (The Correlation Coefficient), Equations 19.5-19.8, pp. 307-308.
#> 
#>  Also: Fisher, R. A. (1921). On the 'probable error' of a coefficient of correlation deduced from a small sample. Metron, 1, 3-32.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 219 participants with complete measurement pairs. With 5% unusable pairs, recruit 231 people; repeated measurements of one person do not replace independent participants.

Chapter 5: Diagnostic Accuracy Studies

5.1 Sensitivity/Specificity Precision & Screening Size

  • Population and decision: A stool-test validation consecutively recruits symptomatic or high-risk patients referred for colonoscopy, with an anticipated target-disease prevalence of 20%. That prevalence is not intended to represent general community screening.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Collect the index-test sample before the reference examination, use a locked threshold, and ascertain disease consistently in all participants while keeping interpretations as independent as feasible.
  • Planning inputs: Target sensitivity prob = 0.85, 95% CI half-width d = 0.05, and prevalence = 0.20 for conversion from confirmed cases to a screening cohort.
  • Why this design: This plans sensitivity precision and therefore requires enough reference-positive cases. If specificity precision is also primary, calculate its non-case requirement and meet both quotas.
  • Formula (Zhou Eq 6.2): \[n_{cases} = \frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{d^2}, \quad N_{screen} = \frac{n_{cases}}{\text{prevalence}}\] Zhou, Obuchowski & McClish (2011), Section 6.1.1, pp. 194-196.
res_5_1 <- calculate("diagAccuracy", "estimate", "proportion", prob = 0.85, d = 0.05, prevalence = 0.20, alpha = 0.05)
print(res_5_1)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Diagnostic accuracy (single)"
#> • Cases needed: 196
#> • Total subjects to screen: 980
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `N_cases = (Z_1-a/2)^2 * P*(1-P)/d^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n_{{{cases}}} = \frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{d^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Specify diagnostic accuracy prob (Se or Sp) = 0.85, margin of error d
#> = 0.05, prevalence = 0.20 (alpha = 0.05).
#> • Step 2: Determine critical value: Z_(1-alpha/2) = 1.96 (confidence level =
#> 95%).
#> • Step 3: Calculate target cases required: n_cases = Z_sum^2 * prob * (1 -
#> prob) / d^2 = (1.96)^2 * 0.85 * 0.15 / (0.05)^2 = 195.91.
#> • Step 4: Adjust for disease prevalence: total subjects to screen = n_cases /
#> prevalence = 195.91 / 0.20 = 979.57.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: Target cases needed = 196, Total subjects to
#> screen = 980.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Hanley, J. A., & McNeil, B. J. (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143(1), 29-36.
#> 
#> Review: Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. Journal of Biomedical Informatics, 48, 193-204.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 196 confirmed cases, with returned average screening size 980. An expected case yield is not a 90% probability guarantee; use Section 5.15 for that recruitment requirement.

5.2 Diagnostic Superiority Test (Asymptotic Method)

  • Population and decision: An imaging team validates a lung-nodule diagnostic model in a referral population using a frozen model and positive threshold, with validation patients separate from development and threshold-selection data.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Compare sensitivity among reference-confirmed malignant cases. Define a patient-level result or one prespecified lesion per patient rather than treating multiple nodules from one person as independent cases.
  • Planning inputs: The protocol adopts minimum acceptable sensitivity p0 = 0.70 and anticipates prob = 0.85. The 70% threshold is an assumption for this study, not a universal industry standard.
  • Why this design: Use an asymptotic one-sided test with α=0.05 and 80% power; assume referral-population prevalence 20% for average screening conversion. Plan specificity separately if required.
  • Formula (Hajian-Tilaki Eq 6.8): \[n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p(1-p)}\right]^2}{(p - p_0)^2}\] 
res_5_2 <- calculate("diagAccuracy", "test", "proportion", prob = 0.85, p0 = 0.70, prevalence = 0.20, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_2)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Diagnostic superiority (single)"
#> • Cases needed: 50
#> • Total subjects to screen: 248
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `N_cases = [Za*sqrt(P0*Q0) + Zb*sqrt(P*Q)]^2 / (P-P0)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p(1-p)}\right]^2}{(p - p_0)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Diagnostic superiority (single).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: prob = 0.85, p0 = 0.70, prevalence = 0.20, alpha =
#> 0.05, power = 0.80, method = asymptotic, alternative = one.sided.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: N_cases = [Za*sqrt(P0*Q0) + Zb*sqrt(P*Q)]^2 /
#> (P-P0)^2.
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Cases needed: 50; Total subjects to
#> screen: 248.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. Journal of Biomedical Informatics, 48, 193-204 (Eq 6.8; the paper uses two-sided Z_alpha/2 throughout, p. 197). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbi.2014.02.013
#> 
#>  One-sided variant: Akoglu, H. (2022). User's guide to sample size estimation in diagnostic accuracy studies. Turkish Journal of Emergency Medicine, 22(4), 177-185 (Table 2, Eq 2, p. 180; one-sided Z_alpha).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 50 disease-positive cases. The unrounded requirement produces a returned screening total of 248; converting the rounded case quota at 20% prevalence gives 250. Allow separately for invalid tests or incomplete reference assessments.

5.3 Diagnostic Superiority Test (A’Hern Exact Method)

  • Population and decision: The same locked-threshold lung-nodule diagnostic model is evaluated with relatively few disease-positive cases, motivating a direct exact-binomial requirement for the number correctly detected.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Each confirmed malignant patient is classified as a true positive or false negative, with reference and unevaluable-result rules fixed before analysis. Do not move the diagnostic model threshold after seeing whether the cutoff is met.
  • Planning inputs: Retain sensitivity 85% versus null 70%, one-sided α=0.05, and 80% power, but specify method = "exact" to search the discrete design.
  • Why this design: Actual error and power need not equal nominal settings exactly. Record actual_alpha, actual_power, and critical_successes along with the sample size.
  • Formula: exact binomial — \(P(X \ge r \mid p_0) \le \alpha\), \(P(X \ge r \mid p) \ge 1-\beta\) (A’Hern 2001).
res_5_3 <- calculate("diagAccuracy", "test", "proportion", prob = 0.85, p0 = 0.70, prevalence = 0.20, method = "exact", alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_3)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Diagnostic superiority (single test, exact binomial)"
#> • Cases needed: 49
#> • Total subjects to screen: 245
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • prob = expected diagnostic sensitivity/specificity
#> • p0 = unacceptable/null sensitivity or specificity threshold
#> • critical_successes = declare superior if correct cases >= 40 of 49
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `exact binomial: P(X >= r | p0) <= alpha and P(X >= r | prob) >= power`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$P(X \ge r \mid p_0) \le \alpha \quad \text{and} \quad P(X \ge r \mid p) \ge 1-\beta$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Diagnostic superiority (single test, exact
#> binomial).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: prob = 0.85, p0 = 0.70, prevalence = 0.20, alpha =
#> 0.05, power = 0.80, method = exact, alternative = one.sided.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: exact binomial: P(X >= r | p0) <= alpha and P(X
#> >= r | prob) >= power.
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Cases needed: 49; Total subjects to
#> screen: 245.
#> Reference:
#> Primary (exact binomial): A'Hern, R. P. (2001). Sample size tables for exact single-stage phase II designs. Statistics in Medicine, 20(6), 859-866. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.721
#> 
#>  Also: Hajian-Tilaki, K. (2014). Sample size estimation in diagnostic test studies of biomedical informatics. Journal of Biomedical Informatics, 48, 193-204.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and decision rule: 49 confirmed cases and at least 40 true-positive classifications. Actual α is 0.048 and power 0.8089; at 20% prevalence, returned average screening size is 245.

5.4 Dual-Endpoint Diagnostic Trial (Se + Sp Co-Primary)

  • Population and decision: An independent breast-lesion diagnostic model validation requires both sensitivity and specificity to exceed their own benchmarks, consecutively enrolling patients scheduled for reference assessment with one defined analysis unit per patient.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Reference-positive patients contribute sensitivity and reference-negative patients contribute specificity. Both endpoints must succeed; omit prevalence when recruiting the two groups by quota; with clinical screening, prevalence converts both quotas separately.
  • Planning inputs: Assume Se of 90% versus null 80%, Sp of 85% versus null 75%, and dual_power = 0.90. Powering each endpoint at 90% supports an approximately 80% lower planning bound for joint success; the actual joint behavior depends on the design. Assume screening prevalence 40%.
  • Why this design: Track case and non-case requirements separately. When screening consecutively, the required enrollment is the maximum of the prevalence-adjusted integer quotas.
  • Formula: \[n_{Se} = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p(1-p)}\right]^2}{(p-p_0)^2}, \quad N_{screen} = \max\left(\left\lceil\frac{n_{Se}}{P}\right\rceil, \left\lceil\frac{n_{Sp}}{1-P}\right\rceil\right)\] 
res_5_4 <- calculate("diagAccuracy", "test", "proportion", prob = 0.90, p0 = 0.80, prob_spec = 0.85, p0_spec = 0.75, prevalence = 0.40, dual = TRUE)
print(res_5_4)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Diagnostic accuracy (dual endpoint: Se + Sp)"
#> • Cases needed: 109
#> • N for sensitivity: 109
#> • N for specificity: 137
#> • Total subjects to screen: 273
#> • Cases needed: 109
#> • Controls needed: 137
#> • Total subjects: 246
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • prob/p0 = expected and null sensitivity
#> • prob_spec/p0_spec = expected and null specificity
#> • dual_power = power for each endpoint; 0.90 gives a joint power lower bound of
#> 0.80 under the endpoint approximations
#> • prevalence = disease proportion for expected screening volume; omit for
#> separate case-control recruitment
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n(p,p0)=[Za*sqrt(p0*(1-p0))+Zb*sqrt(p*(1-p))]^2/(p-p0)^2;
#> N_screen=max(ceil(n_Se/prev),ceil(n_Sp/(1-prev)))`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$N_{screen}=\max\left(\left\lceil\frac{n_{Se}}{P}\right\rceil,\left\lceil\frac{n_{Sp}}{1-P}\right\rceil\right)$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Plan sensitivity 0.9000 vs 0.8000 and specificity 0.8500 vs 0.7500,
#> each with alpha 0.0500 and power 0.9000.
#> • Step 2: Round each endpoint requirement separately: 109 diseased cases and
#> 137 non-diseased controls.
#> • Step 3: Fixed strata quotas total 109 + 137 = 246 participants.
#> • Step 4: At prevalence 0.4000, screen max(ceil(109/0.4000),ceil(137/0.6000)) =
#> 273 participants in expectation; this is not a recruitment assurance
#> probability.
#> Reference:
#> Akoglu, H. (2022). User's guide to sample size estimation in diagnostic accuracy studies. Turkish Journal of Emergency Medicine, 22(4), 177-185 (p. 184; separate sensitivity and specificity requirements).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: Sensitivity requires 109 cases, specificity 137 non-cases, for 246 participants across the two strata. At prevalence 40%, the expected screening requirement is 273 people; account additionally for random case yield.

5.5 Unpaired Comparison of Two Diagnostic Tests

  • Population and decision: Two pneumonia CT-based diagnostic systems are validated in independent patient groups, for example by random allocation from the same source population with each person assigned to one system’s formal assessment.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Apply the same reference process in both groups and compare sensitivity in confirmed pneumonia cases. Severity distribution and reference ascertainment should not systematically differ between groups.
  • Planning inputs: Assume sensitivities p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.75, source prevalence 20%, two-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. This is not a comparison of positivity among all screened patients.
  • Why this design: Use an unpaired two-proportion approach with independent confirmed cases in each group. If both systems evaluate the same patients, switch to paired planning with a discordance assumption.
  • Formula (Fleiss kernel): \[n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{2\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_2)^2}\] 
res_5_5 <- calculate("diagAccuracyCompare", "test", "proportion", p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.75, prevalence = 0.20, paired = FALSE, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_5)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Two diagnostic measures"
#> • Cases needed: 250
#> • Total subjects to screen: 2500

#> `n = [Za/2 * sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Zb * sqrt(p1*(1-p1)+p2*(1-p2))]^2 /
#> (p1-p2)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{2\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)}\right]^2}{(p_1-p_2)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Two diagnostic measures.

#> FALSE, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: n = [Za/2 * sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + Zb *
#> sqrt(p1*(1-p1)+p2*(1-p2))]^2 / (p1-p2)^2.
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Cases needed: 250; Total subjects to
#> screen: 2500.

#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 250 confirmed pneumonia cases per group, with total average screening size 2500. Non-cases can support additional specificity reporting, but this calculation does not separately guarantee specificity precision or power.

5.6 Paired Comparison of Two Diagnostic Tests (Connor Kernel)

  • Population and decision: Both frozen diagnostic model systems now evaluate the same patients’ CT images, and a common reference process establishes pneumonia status.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Compare paired sensitivity only in disease-positive patients, recording both-correct, system-1-only correct, system-2-only correct, and both-incorrect results.
  • Planning inputs: Assume sensitivities 85% versus 75% and psi = 0.10. This equals the minimum discordance compatible with the rate difference and implies no reverse discordance, making it an optimistic assumption; paired pilot data should inform less favorable scenarios.
  • Why this design: Connor planning uses within-patient dependence, with two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power. A diagnostic pair is one patient assessed twice, not two independently recruited cases.
  • Formula (Connor): \[n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\psi} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{\psi-\delta^2}\right]^2}{\delta^2}\] 
res_5_6 <- calculate("diagAccuracyCompare", "test", "proportion", p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.75, prevalence = 0.20, paired = TRUE, psi = 0.10, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_6)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results

#> • Pairs needed: 77
#> • Total subjects to screen: 381
#> • Cases needed: 77
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p1/p2 = expected sensitivities of the two tests
#> • psi = expected discordant-pair proportion (pi10 + pi01)
#> • output is in PAIRS (cases); screening total = pairs/prevalence
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = [Za*sqrt(psi) + Zb*sqrt(psi-delta^2)]^2/delta^2`

#> $$n = \frac{\left[Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\psi} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{\psi-\delta^2}\right]^2}{\delta^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Paired binary parameters: p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.75, discordant pair
#> proportion psi = 0.10, difference delta = |p1 - p2| = 0.10.
#> • Step 2: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 3: Connor formula: n_pairs = [Z_(alpha/2)*sqrt(psi) + Z_beta*sqrt(psi -
#> delta^2)]^2 / delta^2 = 76.09.

#>
  • Result and recruitment: 77 disease-positive patients, each evaluated by both systems. The returned screening conversion is 381; converting the rounded quota at 20% prevalence gives 385 screened patients on average.

5.7 Diagnostic Non-Inferiority (Proportions)

  • Population and decision: A home-sampling assay is compared with a laboratory assay to determine whether reduced sampling burden preserves acceptable sensitivity, using two independent patient groups in this example.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Each group receives its assigned assay and the same reference process. Compare true-positive fractions among confirmed cases; patients assessed by both assays would require consideration of paired covariance instead.
  • Planning inputs: Assume study sensitivity 90%, control sensitivity 88%, maximum acceptable loss margin = 0.05, one-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. Justify the margin in terms of missed cases, convenience, and comparator performance.
  • Why this design: n_per_group is the case requirement in each independent assay group. The screening conversion field describes one group and is not the total recruitment across both groups.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta})^2\left[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)\right]}{(p_1-p_2+\Delta)^2}\] 
res_5_7 <- calculate("diagAccuracyCompare", "noninferiority", "proportion", p1 = 0.90, p2 = 0.88, margin = 0.05, prevalence = 0.30, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_7)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Diagnostic non-inferiority (two proportions)"
#> • Sample size per group: 247
#> • Total sample size: 494
#> • Cases needed: 247
#> • Total subjects to screen: 823
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p1/p2 = expected sensitivities (or specificities) of the new/reference test
#> • margin = non-inferiority/equivalence margin Delta
#> • non-inferiority uses one-sided alpha; equivalence uses Z_{beta/2}
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = (Za+Zb)^2 * (p1q1+p2q2) / (p1-p2+margin)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta})^2\left[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)\right]}{(p_1-p_2+\Delta)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: State non-inferiority hypotheses: H0: p1 - p2 <= -margin vs H1: p1 -
#> p2 > -margin (margin Delta = 0.05, one-sided alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Effective difference: delta_E = p1 - p2 + margin = 0.90 - 0.88 + 0.05
#> = 0.07.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: one-sided Z_alpha = 1.6449, Z_beta =
#> 0.8416.
#> • Step 4: Compute sample size: n = (Z_alpha + Z_beta)^2 * [p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)]
#> / delta_E^2 = 246.80.
#> • Step 5: Round up to integer: n = 247 per group, total sample size N = 494.
#> Reference:
#> Framework: Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Chapter 4, Section 4.2.2 (noninferiority/superiority) and 4.2.3 (equivalence), Eq 4.8-4.9, pp. 78-79. Machin et al. (2018) Ch.11, Eq 11.5-11.6, p. 174.
#> 
#>  Diagnostic application: Zhou, X.-H., Obuchowski, N. A., & McClish, D. K. (2011). Statistical Methods in Diagnostic Medicine (2nd ed.), Section 6.3 (non-inferiority/equivalency of two tests), pp. 214-218.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 247 cases per group, 494 cases across groups. The returned single-group screening conversion is 823; at 30% prevalence, rounded case quotas require about 1648 screened patients across both groups.

5.8 Diagnostic Equivalence (Proportions)

  • Population and decision: A hospital evaluates whether two point-of-care analyzers have sufficiently similar sensitivity, assigning separate patients to independent device groups with a common reference examination.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Use fixed positivity thresholds and standardized specimen handling and quality control. Testing the same specimens on both devices creates a paired study and requires a corresponding method.
  • Planning inputs: Assume p1 = 0.90, p2 = 0.89, equivalence bounds ±0.05, one-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. The acceptable difference must reflect the particular disease and consequences of missed diagnoses.
  • Why this design: Equivalence excludes unacceptable differences in both directions. A nonsignificant ordinary comparison is not evidence that the devices are interchangeable.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta/2})^2\left[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)\right]}{(\Delta-|p_1-p_2|)^2}\] 
res_5_8 <- calculate("diagAccuracyCompare", "equivalence", "proportion", p1 = 0.90, p2 = 0.89, margin = 0.05, prevalence = 0.30, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_8)

5.9 ROC Area Under the Curve (AUC) Precision (Binormal Model)

  • Population and decision: A biomarker team validates the discrimination of a frozen continuous risk score, recruiting reference-confirmed cases and non-cases in a 1:1 ratio from the same intended clinical population.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Each patient contributes one score, and ROC-AUC summarizes ranking discrimination. Non-cases should resemble actual clinical comparators rather than exclusively healthy volunteers compared with advanced cases.
  • Planning inputs: Assume AUC=0.80, 95% CI half-width d = 0.10, ratio = 1, and var_method = "binormal". Inform the AUC and variance choice using independent pilot or external validation data.
  • Why this design: This estimates AUC precision with investigator-set disease quotas. Such a quota sample does not directly estimate population prevalence or unweighted positive predictive value.
  • Formula (Obuchowski 1994 binormal variance, Zhou Eq 6.5): \[n_{cases} = \left(\frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}}{d}\right)^2 \cdot V(AUC), \quad V = 0.0099\,e^{-a^2/2}\left[(5a^2+8) + \frac{a^2+8}{R}\right],\ a = \sqrt{2}\,\Phi^{-1}(A)\] 
res_5_9 <- calculate("diagAUC", "estimate", "auc", auc = 0.80, d = 0.10, ratio = 1, var_method = "binormal", alpha = 0.05)
print(res_5_9)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Single-group AUC CI precision"
#> • Cases needed: 46
#> • Controls needed: 46
#> • Total subjects: 92
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • auc = anticipated area under the ROC curve
#> • precision = desired CI half-width L
#> • ratio = controls per case (non-cases:cases; default 1)
#> • prevalence = clinical disease proportion; alternative to fixed ratio
#> • screening totals, when present, meet expected case and control quotas, not an
#> assurance probability
#> • var_method = binormal variance function
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `N_cases = (Z_1-a/2 / d)^2 * V(AUC); controls = ceiling(ceiling(N_cases)*R), R
#> = controls/cases`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n_{cases} = \left(\frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}}{d}\right)^2 \cdot V(AUC), \quad R = n_{controls}/n_{cases}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Anticipated AUC = 0.80, precision d = 0.10, controls:cases R = 1,
#> alpha = 0.05.
#> • Step 2: Use the binormal variance model: V(AUC) = 0.1195.
#> • Step 3: Calculate cases: n_cases = (Z_(1-alpha/2)/d)^2 * V(AUC) =
#> (1.96/0.10)^2 * 0.1195 = 45.89.
#> • Step 4: Round cases up first: Target cases needed = 46; controls =
#> ceiling(cases*R) = 46.
#> • Step 5: Sum integer quotas: Total subjects = 46 + 46 = 92.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Zhou, X.-H., Obuchowski, N. A., & McClish, D. K. (2011). Statistical Methods in Diagnostic Medicine (2nd ed.). Wiley. Section 6.1.2, pp. 196-199 (Eq 6.4/6.5/6.6; CTC worked example).
#> 
#>  Original variance: Hanley, J. A., & McNeil, B. J. (1982). Radiology, 143(1), 29-36.
#>  Binormal variance: Obuchowski, N. A. (1994). Computing sample size for receiver operating characteristic studies. Investigative Radiology, 29(2), 238-243.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 46 cases and the same number of non-cases, 92 total. Meet both disease-status quotas; a sufficient total with too few cases does not meet this precision plan.

5.10 ROC-AUC Superiority Test

  • Population and decision: A team validates an independent miRNA score against a prespecified minimum useful discrimination level, rather than merely testing whether it exceeds random ranking at AUC=0.5.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Freeze the algorithm before collecting continuous scores and reference disease status, handling cases and non-cases consistently. The primary endpoint is the overall ROC-AUC.
  • Planning inputs: Assume auc = 0.80, minimum acceptable auc0 = 0.70, source prevalence 30%, two-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. Justify the minimum for the intended application.
  • Why this design: An AUC test does not automatically guarantee sensitivity, specificity at an operating threshold, or calibration. Plan those separately if they are also primary objectives.
  • Formula: \[n_{cases} = \frac{\left(Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{V(AUC_0)} + Z_{\beta}\sqrt{V(AUC)}\right)^2}{(AUC - AUC_0)^2}\] 
res_5_10 <- calculate("diagAUC", "test", "auc", auc = 0.80, auc0 = 0.70, prevalence = 0.30, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_10)

  • Result and recruitment: 82 cases, with an average screening size of 275. Non-cases also contribute to AUC estimation, so recruiting cases alone does not satisfy the design.

5.11 Two ROC-AUC Comparison

  • Population and decision: A liver-lesion study obtains two imaging scores from the same patients and uses a common reference standard to compare two correlated ROC-AUC estimates.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Retain patient-level pairing between the continuous scores, with reference interpretation as independent as feasible from either study score.
  • Planning inputs: Assume AUCs 0.80 and 0.70 and r=0.50, where r is correlation between AUC estimators, not ordinary Pearson correlation between raw scores. Use compatible paired pilot data to inform it.
  • Why this design: Use two-sided α=0.05, 80% power, and assumed prevalence 30%. Completing both examinations provides paired information; it does not create two independent patients.
  • Formula: \[n_{cases} = \frac{2(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2 \cdot V(AUC) \cdot (1-r)}{(AUC_1 - AUC_2)^2}\] Hajian-Tilaki (2014), Eqs 7.6/7.8.
res_5_11 <- calculate("diagAUCCompare", "test", "auc", auc1 = 0.80, auc2 = 0.70, r = 0.50, prevalence = 0.30, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_11)

5.12 Two ROC-AUC Non-Inferiority

  • Population and decision: A hospital evaluates a portable, lower-cost scoring device for preservation of the standard device’s discrimination, arranging equal case and non-case quotas and obtaining both scores from each patient.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Generate both continuous scores with locked algorithms, construct ROC curves against the same disease reference, and retain patient pairing.
  • Planning inputs: Assume study AUC=0.85, reference AUC=0.82, r=0.50, maximum loss margin = 0.05, one-sided α=0.05, and 80% power.
  • Why this design: Justify the AUC margin for the intended use. This branch uses equal case/non-case allocation in its variance calculation; its total is not derived from natural clinical prevalence.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{2(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta})^2 V(1-r)}{(AUC_1-AUC_2+\Delta)^2}\] 
res_5_12 <- calculate("diagAUCCompare", "noninferiority", "auc", auc1 = 0.85, auc2 = 0.82, r = 0.50, margin = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_12)

5.13 Two ROC-AUC Equivalence

  • Population and decision: Two diagnostic model scores are evaluated for sufficiently similar AUCs on the same clinical validation sample, with cases and non-cases recruited in equal proportions.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Each patient receives both frozen continuous scores, and paired AUC differences are calculated against the same disease reference. AUCs from independent hospital samples are not correlated estimates merely because they use similar patients.
  • Planning inputs: Assume AUCs 0.85 and 0.84, r=0.50, equivalence bounds ±0.05, one-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. Variance-model and correlation assumptions materially affect the requirement.
  • Why this design: The objective excludes both unacceptable directions of AUC difference. AUC equivalence alone does not establish interchangeability at every threshold or clinical decision.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{2(Z_{\alpha}+Z_{\beta/2})^2 V(1-r)}{(\Delta-|AUC_1-AUC_2|)^2}\] 
res_5_13 <- calculate("diagAUCCompare", "equivalence", "auc", auc1 = 0.85, auc2 = 0.84, r = 0.50, margin = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_5_13)

5.14 Negative Likelihood Ratio Threshold Precision

  • Population and decision: An emergency team independently validates a fixed-threshold D-dimer pathway, focusing on how a negative result changes pulmonary embolism probability and initially planning equal confirmed case and non-case quotas.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Ascertain disease consistently, estimate sensitivity and specificity, and plan the upper log-scale CI limit for LR−=(1−Se)/Sp rather than a fixed-width sensitivity CI.
  • Planning inputs: Assume Se=0.90 and Sp=0.50, giving anticipated LR−=0.20; target an approximate 95% upper limit of target_lr = 0.40 at those anticipated parameters. Justify the target using pretest probability and the intended decision.
  • Why this design: With equal groups, the variance coefficient is 0.9/0.1+0.5/0.5=10 and the target log distance is log(0.4/0.2). This is approximate precision planning, not 95% assurance that every realized study CI meets the target.
  • Formula (Simel 1991 log-CI): \[\log(LR^-) \pm Z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{Se}{n(1-Se)} + \frac{1-Sp}{n\cdot Sp}}\] Hajian-Tilaki (2014), Section 6.4, Eqs 6.13/6.14.
res_5_14 <- calculate("diagLR", "estimate", "lr", sens = 0.90, spec = 0.50, target_lr = 0.40, lr_type = "negative", alpha = 0.05)
print(res_5_14)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Likelihood ratio (negative, log-CI method)"
#> • Cases needed: 80
#> • Controls needed: 80
#> • Total subjects: 160
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • sens/spec = expected sensitivity/specificity (determine the observed LR)
#> • target_lr = LR boundary the CI must not cross (precision target)
#> • n is computed per group (equal cases and controls)
#> ! Plans the approximate CI limit at the anticipated Se/Sp to reach target_lr;
#> ! this is a precision calculation, not a guarantee about every realized CI.
#> ! distinct from fixed-width CI approaches (e.g. prec_lr in presize).
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `log(LR-) +- Z * sqrt(Se/(n*(1-Se)) + (1-Sp)/(n*Sp))`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$\log(LR^-) \pm Z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{Se}{n(1-Se)} + \frac{1-Sp}{n \cdot Sp}}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Expected negative LR = 0.200000 from sensitivity 0.9000 and

#> 0.399922.

#>

#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 80 confirmed pulmonary embolism cases and 80 non-cases, 160 total. These are disease-status quotas, not total consecutive emergency attendees; a consecutive design must additionally account for local prevalence and the yield of both groups.

5.15 Guaranteed Screening Target (screen_required)

  • Population and decision: A colorectal referral cohort needs 196 reference-positive cases and anticipates prevalence 20%, so the team must decide how many complete test-and-reference appointments to prepare.
  • Procedures and endpoint: With a fixed consecutively enrolled total, the number of cases varies around its expectation. Screening 980 people gives an expected 196 cases, not a high-probability guarantee of that many.
  • Planning inputs: Use n = 196, prevalence = 0.20, and beta = 0.10 as the tolerated probability of insufficient cases. This beta concerns recruitment yield, distinct from type-II error in an accuracy hypothesis test.
  • Why this design: Find the smallest total meeting the binomial tail requirement, assuming approximately independent disease status and stable source prevalence. Enrichment or stratified quotas require their corresponding recruitment assumptions.
  • Formula: \[P(\text{Binomial}(N, \text{prevalence}) \ge n) \ge 1-\beta\] Zhou et al. (2011), Eq 6.3.
safe_n <- screen_required(n = 196, prevalence = 0.20, beta = 0.10)
cat("Average screening target: 980; 90% guaranteed enrollment target:", safe_n, "\n")
#> Average screening target: 980; 90% guaranteed enrollment target: 1061
  • Result and recruitment: Prepare 1061 complete participants, 81 more than the expectation-based total. Under these assumptions the chance of at least 196 cases is 90.09%. Incomplete reference examinations require additional operational allowance.

5.16 Multi-Reader Multi-Case (MRMC) Power Analysis

  • Population and decision: An imaging study compares two breast-imaging techniques using 8 radiologists and the same 50 patients, accounting for both patient and reader variability.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Randomize reading order, control memory effects between sessions, and blind readers to reference status. Each reader evaluates both techniques for each patient.
  • Planning inputs: Reuse the Zhou textbook mammography planning components: AUC difference delta = 0.10, reader/occasion/patient-sampling variances 0.00123, 0.00087, and 0.00196, and correlations rho1 = 0.5, rho2 = 0.3, rho3 = 0.25, rho_b = 0.75. These require compatible MRMC pilot information and are not replaceable by the SD of a single AUC estimate.
  • Why this design: mrmc_power() evaluates power at fixed patient and reader counts; it does not solve for minimum enrollment. One reading occasion entails 50×8×2=800 interpretations.
  • Formula (non-central \(F\), Zhou Eq 6.32): \[\lambda = \frac{J\delta^2}{2\left[\sigma_b^2(1-\rho_b) + \sigma_w^2/Q + \sigma_c^2\left((1-\rho_1)+(J-1)(\rho_2-\rho_3)\right)\right]}, \quad \text{power} = P(F_{1,J-1}(\lambda) > F_{1-\alpha})\] Zhou et al. (2011), Section 6.5, Eq 6.32, p. 221 (worked example p. 225).
res_5_16 <- mrmc_power(n = 50, J = 8, delta = 0.10, sigma_b2 = 0.00123, sigma_w2 = 0.00087, sigma_c2 = 0.00196, rho1 = 0.50, rho2 = 0.30, rho3 = 0.25, rho_b = 0.75)
print(res_5_16)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "MRMC (paired-patient, paired-reader, Obuchowski-Rockette)"
#> • Cases needed: 50
#> • Power achieved: 0.893
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • n = patients with the condition (paired-patient: imaged under both tests)
#> • J = readers per test
#> • delta = accuracy difference to detect
#> • sigma_b2/sigma_w2/sigma_c2 = reader/occasion/patient-sampling variance
#> components
#> • rho1/rho2/rho3 = correlations (same-reader-diff-test / diff-reader-same-test
#> / diff-reader-diff-test)
#> • rho_b = same-reader, different-test correlation (Table 6.3 p_b)
#> ! MRMC power depends on 6 variance/correlation components estimated from
#> ! pilot data or literature (Zhou Table 6.3); treat results as approximate.
#> ! sigma_c2 is the patient-sampling variance component V(A)/n (Zhou p. 221),
#> ! so it already reflects the patient sample size; it is not divided by n again.
#> ! rho_b is the same-reader, different-test correlation (Table 6.3 `p_b`);
#> ! when omitted it defaults to rho1.
#> ! For reader variability planning: sigma_b2 = (accuracy range / 4)^2 is a
#> ! common heuristic (Zhou p. 223, Beam 1996 mammography example).
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `lambda = J*delta^2/(2*[sb2(1-rho_b) + sw2/Q +
#> sc2*((1-rho1)+(J-1)(rho2-rho3))]); power = P(F_{1,J-1}(lambda) > F_{1-alpha})`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$\lambda = \frac{J \delta^2}{2\left[\sigma_b^2(1-\rho_b) + \frac{\sigma_w^2}{Q} + \sigma_c^2\left((1-\rho_1) + (J-1)(\rho_2-\rho_3)\right)\right]}, \quad \text{Power} = P(F_{1,J-1}(\lambda) > F_{1-\alpha})$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: MRMC (paired-patient, paired-reader,
#> Obuchowski-Rockette).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: n = 50, J = 8, delta = 0.10, sigma_b2 = 0.0012,
#> sigma_w2 = 0.0009, sigma_c2 = 0.002, rho1 = 0.50, rho2 = 0.30, rho3 = 0.25,
#> rho_b = 0.75, rho_b_defaulted = FALSE, alpha = 0.05, n_repeats = 1,
#> noncentrality_lambda = 14.0672.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: lambda = J*delta^2/(2*[sb2(1-rho_b) + sw2/Q +
#> sc2*((1-rho1)+(J-1)(rho2-rho3))]); power = P(F_{1,J-1}(lambda) > F_{1-alpha}).
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Cases needed: 50; Power achieved:
#> 0.893.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Zhou, X.-H., Obuchowski, N. A., & McClish, D. K. (2011). Statistical Methods in Diagnostic Medicine (2nd ed.). Wiley. Section 6.5, Eq 6.32, Tables 6.3-6.5, pp. 220-226 (mammography worked example: 89% power).
#> 
#>  Model: Obuchowski, N. A., & Rockette, H. E. (1995). Hypothesis testing of diagnostic accuracy for multiple readers and multiple tests: an ANOVA approach with dependent observations. Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation, 24(2), 285-308.
#> 
#>  Method review: Obuchowski, N. A., Beiden, S. V., Berbaum, K. S., Hillis, S. L., Ishwaran, H., Song, H. H., & Wagner, R. F. (2004). Multireader, multicase receiver operating characteristic analysis: an empirical comparison of five methods. Academic Radiology, 11(9), 980-995.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and workload: Calculated power is 89.3%. Recalculate if reader availability, case spectrum, or variance components change; maintaining only the same total number of interpretations is insufficient.

Chapter 6: Complex and Modern Trial Designs

6.1 Cluster Randomized Trial (Continuous Outcome)

  • Population and decision: A multicenter ICU study randomizes wards to a care workflow to reduce contamination between patients treated by the same staff, with about 20 eligible patients per ward.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Define a patient-level continuous recovery score with higher values indicating benefit, standardized timing, and assessor training. Assume control mean 10 and intervention mean 12.
  • Planning inputs: Use patient-level SD=3, icc = 0.05, and cluster_size = 20, giving design effect 1.95. ICC evidence should match the ward structure, outcome, and recruitment period.
  • Why this design: The function applies the design effect to the individually randomized requirement, adds Machin’s Student t correction, and rounds once at the cluster level (each extra cluster adds a further m patients). Also assess whether the cluster count, unequal sizes, and intended cluster or mixed-model analysis support the actual trial.
  • Formula (Machin Eq 12.10, p. 199): \[DE = 1 + (m-1)\rho, \quad N = DE\left[\frac{(1+\varphi)^2}{\varphi}\cdot\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2}{(\delta/\sigma)^2} + \frac{Z^2_{\alpha/2}}{2}\right], \quad K = \left\lceil \frac{N/(1+\varphi)}{m} \right\rceil\] Machin et al. (2018), Ch. 12, Eq 12.4-12.13, pp. 197-200; Donner & Klar (2000).
res_6_1 <- calculate("clusterRCT", "test", "mean", mean1 = 10, mean2 = 12, sd = 3, icc = 0.05, cluster_size = 20, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_6_1)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Cluster RCT: two independent samples, mean comparison"
#> • Sample size per group: 80
#> • Total sample size: 160
#> • Clusters per arm: 4
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • mean1/mean2 = group means; sd = common SD (individual level)
#> • icc = intra-cluster correlation rho (Machin Eq 12.4)
#> • cluster_size = subjects per cluster m
#> • DE = 1+(m-1)*ICC = 1.9500; n_clusters per arm = 4
#> ! Machin Eq 12.10 includes the Student t correction z^2/2 and rounds once
#> ! at the cluster level; each extra cluster adds a further m subjects.
#> ! For variable cluster sizes use Eq 12.6-12.7 (cv_m) and Eq 12.8.
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `N = DE*[(1+phi)^2/phi*(Za/2+Zb)^2/(delta/sigma)^2 + Za/2^2/2], DE =
#> 1+(m-1)*ICC`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$N = DE\left[\frac{(1+\varphi)^2}{\varphi}\cdot\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2}{(\delta/\sigma)^2} + \frac{Z^2_{\alpha/2}}{2}\right], \quad DE = 1+(m-1)\rho$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Compute individual-level sample size without clustering from standard
#> two-group formulas.
#> • Step 2: Calculate design effect (inflation factor): DE = 1 + (cluster_size -
#> 1) * ICC = 1 + (20 - 1) * 0.05 = 1.95.
#> • Step 3: Inflate sample size for clustering: n_clustered = n_individual * DE.
#> • Step 4: Determine clusters required per arm: n_clusters = ceiling(n_clustered
#> / cluster_size) = 4.
#> • Step 5: Total individuals per arm = 4 * 20 = 80; Total sample size N = 160.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Machin, D., Campbell, M. J., Tan, S. B., & Tan, S. H. (2018). Sample Sizes for Clinical, Laboratory and Epidemiology Studies (4th ed.). Wiley. Chapter 12 (Cluster Designs): Eq 12.4 (ICC), Eq 12.5 (DE), Eq 12.9-12.10 (sample size with the Student t correction), pp. 197-199; Example 12.1, p. 206 (N=171.35 -> 172, K=86).
#> 
#>  Also: Donner, A., & Klar, N. (2000). Design and Analysis of Cluster Randomisation Trials in Health Research. Arnold.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 4 wards and 80 patients per arm, 8 wards and 160 patients overall. Plan ward-level losses at the cluster level; adding patients in only a few wards does not replace additional independent wards.

6.2 Cluster Randomized Trial (Binary Outcome)

  • Population and decision: A public-health team randomizes villages to appointment reminders and education to improve screening uptake in eligible residents, reducing within-village intervention spillover.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Recruit 20 eligible residents per village using a prespecified procedure and verify completion of one valid screen within a fixed 6-month window, yielding one binary outcome per resident.
  • Planning inputs: Assume uptake 20% versus 30%, icc = 0.05, cluster_size = 20, two-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. Eligibility and observation windows should match the source data.
  • Why this design: Inflate the two-proportion requirement and round to whole villages. Unequal village sizes or stratified randomization warrant assessment against the final analysis design.
  • Formula: same design effect applied to the two-proportion kernel.
res_6_2 <- calculate("clusterRCT", "test", "proportion", p1 = 0.30, p2 = 0.20, icc = 0.05, cluster_size = 20, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_6_2)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Cluster RCT: two independent proportions"
#> • Sample size per group: 580
#> • Total sample size: 1160
#> • Clusters per arm: 29
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • p1/p2 = group proportions; pbar = (p1+p2)/2
#> • icc = intra-cluster correlation rho_Binary (Machin Eq 12.13)
#> • cluster_size = subjects per cluster m
#> • DE = 1+(m-1)*ICC = 1.9500; n_clusters per arm = 29
#> ! Machin Eq 12.10 includes the Student t correction z^2/2 and rounds once
#> ! at the cluster level; each extra cluster adds a further m subjects.
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `N = DE*[(1+phi)^2/phi*(Za/2+Zb)^2/(delta/sigma_Plan)^2 + Za/2^2/2], sigma_Plan
#> = sqrt(pbar(1-pbar))`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$N = DE\left[\frac{(1+\varphi)^2}{\varphi}\cdot\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2}{(\delta/\sigma_{Plan})^2} + \frac{Z^2_{\alpha/2}}{2}\right], \quad \sigma_{Plan}=\sqrt{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Compute individual-level sample size without clustering from standard
#> two-group formulas.
#> • Step 2: Calculate design effect (inflation factor): DE = 1 + (cluster_size -
#> 1) * ICC = 1 + (20 - 1) * 0.05 = 1.95.
#> • Step 3: Inflate sample size for clustering: n_clustered = n_individual * DE.
#> • Step 4: Determine clusters required per arm: n_clusters = ceiling(n_clustered
#> / cluster_size) = 29.
#> • Step 5: Total individuals per arm = 29 * 20 = 580; Total sample size N =
#> 1160.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Machin, D., Campbell, M. J., Tan, S. B., & Tan, S. H. (2018). Sample Sizes for Clinical, Laboratory and Epidemiology Studies (4th ed.). Wiley. Chapter 12 (Cluster Designs): Eq 12.5 (DE), Eq 12.10 (sample size with the Student t correction), Eq 12.12 (sigma_Plan for a binary outcome), Eq 12.13 (rho_Binary), pp. 197-200; Example 12.4, p. 208.
#> 
#>  Also: Donner, A., & Klar, N. (2000). Design and Analysis of Cluster Randomisation Trials in Health Research. Arnold.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 29 villages and 580 residents per arm, 58 villages and 1160 residents total. Budget village coordination and resident follow-up separately, including procedures for villages that miss their target size.

6.3 Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Trial

  • Population and decision: Twenty-four counties sequentially implement hand hygiene, with randomized switching order in batches of 6. Four switches plus baseline create 5 observation periods, and all counties ultimately receive the intervention.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Sample about 100 new neonates per county per period and ascertain infection in a fixed window. This is repeated cross-sectional sampling, not 5 repeated observations of the same neonates; the binary endpoint is planned using an additive risk-difference approximation.
  • Planning inputs: Set theta = -0.016, between-county variance tau2 = 2.25e-4, individual variance sigma2_ind = 0.0475 (about 5% baseline risk), and m = 100.
  • Why this design: Evaluate power for a fixed cluster, period, and sample configuration. The implemented simplified formula does not explicitly fit a full calendar-time trend; seasonal or secular changes require a model or simulation including those effects.
  • Formula (Hussey & Hughes Eq 8): \[Var(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{I \tau^2 (\tau^2 + T\sigma^2)}{(IU - W)\tau^2 + (U^2 + ITU - TW - IV)\sigma^2}, \quad \text{power} = \Phi\left(|\theta|/SE - z_{1-\alpha/2}\right)\] Hussey & Hughes (2007), Contemp Clin Trials 28(2), 182-191.
res_6_3 <- calculate("steppedWedge", "test", "mean", theta = -0.016, tau2 = 2.25e-4, sigma2_ind = 0.0475, m = 100, n_clusters = 24, clusters_per_step = 6, alpha = 0.05)
print(res_6_3)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Stepped wedge cluster trial (Hussey-Hughes, mean outcome)"
#> • Total clusters: 24
#> • Power achieved: 0.674
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • theta = treatment effect (additive scale; e.g. risk difference)
#> • tau2 = between-cluster variance (e.g. (CV*mean)^2)
#> • sigma2_ind = individual-level variance (binary: p(1-p))
#> • m = individuals sampled per cluster per time point
#> • clusters_per_step = clusters randomized at each step (full design)
#> ! Hussey & Hughes (2007) Eq 8 assumes no underlying calendar time trends.
#> ! If secular time trends are present, statistical power may be lower;
#> ! consider incorporating time fixed effects via simulation or swCRTdesign.
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `Var = I*s2*(s2 + T*t2)/((I*U-W)*s2 + (U^2+I*T*U-T*W-I*V)*t2); power =
#> Phi(|theta|/se - z)`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{I \sigma^2(\sigma^2+T\tau^2)}{(IU-W)\sigma^2 + (U^2+ITU-TW-IV)\tau^2}, \quad \sigma^2 = \sigma_{ind}^2/m, \quad \text{Power} = \Phi\left(\frac{|\theta|}{\text{SE}} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\right)$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Stepped wedge cluster trial (Hussey-Hughes,
#> mean outcome).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: theta = -0.016, tau2 = 0.0002, sigma2_ind = 0.0475,
#> m = 100, n_clusters = 24, clusters_per_step = 6, alpha = 0.05.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: Var = I*s2*(s2 + T*t2)/((I*U-W)*s2 +
#> (U^2+I*T*U-T*W-I*V)*t2); power = Phi(|theta|/se - z).
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Clusters per arm: 24; Power achieved:
#> 0.674.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Hussey, M. A., & Hughes, J. P. (2007). Design and analysis of stepped wedge cluster randomized trials. Contemporary Clinical Trials, 28(2), 182-191 (Eq 8, p. 187; EPT worked example I=24, T=5, m=100, p=0.05, CV=0.3 -> ~80% power at a 36% relative reduction).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and workload: Calculated power is 67.4%. With different neonates each period, budget 24×5×100=12000 observations, together with switching training, period definitions, and complete county-period data.

6.4 Ordered Categorical Outcome (Whitehead Model)

  • Population and decision: A 1:1 randomized osteoarthritis trial compares a study injection with control using pain improvement at week 12, classified as small, moderate, or large improvement.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Define category thresholds in advance and obtain one ordered patient-level outcome using the same scale and scoring procedures. Category order must be consistent with the anticipated treatment direction.
  • Planning inputs: Assume pooled category distribution prop_bar = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3), common or = 1.5, two-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. The distribution is the combined planning distribution, not an arbitrary single-arm set of rates.
  • Why this design: Whitehead’s approximation assumes a common proportional odds effect across cutpoints. Effects concentrated in a particular category require assessment under an appropriate alternative distribution.
  • Formula (Whitehead 1993): \[N = \frac{3(1+\varphi)^2\,(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2}{\varphi\,(\log OR)^2\,(1-\sum \bar{p}_j^3)}, \quad \varphi = n_{test}/n_{standard} = 1\] 
res_6_4 <- calculate("twoOrdinal", "test", "ordinal", or = 1.5, prop_bar = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3), alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_6_4)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Two-group ordered categorical outcome (Mann-Whitney /
#> proportional odds)"
#> • Sample size per group: 342
#> • Standard group: 342
#> • Test group: 342
#> • Total sample size: 684
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • or = anticipated odds ratio (proportional odds)
#> • prop_bar = anticipated average category proportions (sums to 1)
#> • allocation = test:standard sample size ratio; each arm is rounded up
#> separately
#> • total_n = n_standard + n_test after rounding
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `N = Gamma*(1+phi)^2/phi*(Za/2+Zb)^2/(log OR)^2 ; Gamma = 3/(1 - sum(p_bar^3))`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$N = \frac{\Gamma\,(1+\phi)^2}{\phi}\cdot\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2}+Z_{\beta})^2}{(\log OR)^2}, \quad \Gamma = \frac{3}{1-\sum_j \bar{p}_j^3}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Specify odds ratio OR = 1.50, pooled proportion categories = [0.20,
#> 0.50, 0.30].
#> • Step 2: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96, Z_beta = 0.8416.
#> • Step 3: Compute Whitehead variance factor: 1 - sum(p_bar_j^3).
#> • Step 4: Whitehead/Machin formula: N = 3*(1+allocation)^2/allocation *
#> (Z_(alpha/2)+Z_beta)^2 / [(ln OR)^2*(1-sum(p_bar^3))].
#> • Step 5: Round each arm up: Standard group = 342, Test group = 342; sum to
#> Total sample size N = 684.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Whitehead, J. (1993). Sample size calculations for ordered categorical data. Statistics in Medicine, 12(24), 2257-2271 (Eq 9-10, p. 2260; Example 1, p. 2261).
#> 
#>  Book: Machin, D., Campbell, M. J., Tan, S. B., & Tan, S. H. (2018). Sample Sizes for Clinical, Laboratory and Epidemiology Studies (4th ed.). Wiley. Chapter 4, Eq 4.3-4.4, p. 57; Example 4.1, p. 59.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: Each group is rounded up to 342; the reported total 684 is the sum of the integer group sizes. Add any allowance for missing endpoints separately.

6.5 Clinical Prediction Model Development (Riley 2020 BMJ Binary)

  • Population and decision: An ICU team develops a model predicting in-hospital death at admission, consecutively enrolling eligible first admissions and using predictors available at the intended prediction time.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Each patient has one admission outcome. Count parameters needed for categorical expansions, splines, and interactions; 10 parameters need not mean 10 raw variables.
  • Planning inputs: Assume outcome proportion prev = 0.30, n_parameters = 10, anticipated Cox–Snell R²=0.10, target shrinkage 0.90, and overall-risk precision 0.05. External performance estimates should be relevant and adjusted for optimism.
  • Why this design: This branch takes the maximum of overall-risk precision B1, shrinkage B3, and Nagelkerke R² optimism B4. B2 MAPE is informational for at most 30 parameters; machine-learning tuning and external validation need separate planning.
  • Formula (Riley 2020, criteria B1, B3, B4): \[n_{B1} = \left(\frac{z}{\delta}\right)^2 \phi(1-\phi), \quad n(S) = \frac{P}{(S-1)\ln(1-R^2_{CS}/S)}\] \[S_4 = \frac{R^2_{CS}}{R^2_{CS}+0.05\max(R^2_{CS})}, \quad n = \max\{n_{B1}, n(S), n(S_4)\}\] Riley et al. (2020), BMJ 368, m441 (B1, B3, and B4).
res_6_5 <- calculate("predictiveModel", "plan", "binary", prev = 0.30, n_parameters = 10, r2_cs = 0.10, shrinkage = 0.90, precision_delta = 0.05, alpha = 0.05)
print(res_6_5)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Prediction model development (Riley 2020, binary)"
#> • Required sample size: 850
#> • Events required: 255
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • prev = anticipated outcome proportion in the target population
#> • n_parameters = candidate predictor parameters (P)
#> • r2_cs = anticipated Cox-Snell R2 (conservative, optimism-adjusted)
#> • shrinkage = target uniform shrinkage factor S (default 0.9)
#> • mape = mean absolute prediction error for the informational B2 calculation
#> only (default 0.05)
#> ! B1 (proportion precision, delta=0.050): n = 323
#> ! B3 (shrinkage S=0.90, R2cs=0.1000): n = 850
#> ! B2 (MAPE=0.050, P=10 <= 30): n = 461 (informational)
#> ! B4 (Nagelkerke R2 optimism <= 0.05, S=0.7393): n = 264
#> ! Returned n is max(B1, B3, B4); B2 is informational only.
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `B1: n=(z/d)^2*p(1-p); B3/B4: n=P/((S-1)*ln(1-R2cs/S));

#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n(S) = \frac{P}{(S-1)\ln(1-R_{CS}^2/S)}, \quad S_{B4} = \frac{R_{CS}^2}{R_{CS}^2+0.05\max(R_{CS}^2)}, \quad n = \max(n_{B1},n_{B3},n_{B4})$$

#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Prediction model development (Riley 2020,

#> • Step 2: Input parameters: prev = 0.30, n_parameters = 10, r2_cs = 0.10,

#> = 0.05.

#> 
#>  B2 formula: van Smeden, M., et al. (2019). Stat Methods Med Res, 28, 2455-74. B3 derivation: Riley et al. (2019). Stat Med, 38, 1276-96 (PART II). Software: pmsampsize (Stata/R).
