  • Result and recruitment: 850 patients with about 255 expected deaths at the assumed rate. Document which criteria are covered, internal validation, and missing-predictor handling; splitting the development sample does not create an independent external validation study.

6.6 Clinical Prediction Model Development (Riley 2020 Rate)

  • Population and decision: A cardiovascular cohort plans a model for 10-year mortality risk and first assesses how much observed time at risk is needed to estimate the overall baseline cumulative incidence.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Record time from entry to death or censoring, approximating the overall event process by a constant hazard so that 10-year risk is 1−exp(−rate×10).
  • Planning inputs: Assume rate = 0.10 events per person-year, timepoint = 10 years, and two-sided 95% CI errors no larger than precision_delta = 0.05. Align the rate and time units.
  • Why this design: This addresses overall-risk precision criterion T1, not all model-development requirements. Extrapolation from shorter observation to 10 years relies especially strongly on the assumed hazard model.
  • Formula (criterion T1): \(F(t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}\); find person-years \(T\) such that both CI margins of \(F(t)\) stay within \(\delta\).
res_6_6 <- calculate("predictiveModel", "plan", "rate", rate = 0.10, timepoint = 10, precision_delta = 0.05, alpha = 0.05)
print(res_6_6)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Prediction model development (Riley 2020, time-to-event)"
#> • Required person-time: 2366
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • rate = anticipated event rate per person-year
#> • timepoint = key prediction time point t (years)
#> • precision_delta = maximum margin of error for F(t)
#> • n_parameters/epv = optional EPP cross-check (classic 10 EPV)
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `F(t) = 1-exp(-rate*t); CI: 1-exp(-(rate +- z*sqrt(rate/T))*t); find T with
#> margins <= delta`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$F(t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}, \quad \text{CI: } 1 - \exp\left(-\left(\lambda \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{T}}\right)t\right)$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Prediction model development (Riley 2020,
#> time-to-event).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: rate = 0.10, timepoint = 10, precision_delta =
#> 0.05, alpha = 0.05.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: F(t) = 1-exp(-rate*t); CI: 1-exp(-(rate +-
#> z*sqrt(rate/T))*t); find T with margins <= delta.
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Required person-time: 2366.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Riley, R. D., Ensor, J., Snell, K. I. E., et al. (2020). Calculating the sample size required for developing a clinical prediction model. BMJ, 368, m441 (Figure 1, time-to-event panel; criterion T1; worked example: rate=0.10/year, t=10y, delta=0.05 -> 2366 person-years).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: 2366 person-years at risk. If each patient contributes an average of 5 observed years at risk, an initial resource estimate is 474 patients; events, censoring, accrual, and other development criteria determine the actual requirement.

6.7 Prediction Model Development (Classic EPV)

  • Population and decision: At an early grant-planning stage, investigators want a rough cohort size for a binary mortality prediction model containing 10 predictor parameters.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Each patient contributes one complete hospital outcome, and events are deaths. Include coefficients for categorical levels, interactions, and nonlinear effects in the parameter count.
  • Planning inputs: Use epv = 10, n_parameters = 10, and event_prevalence = 0.30, calculating events first and then converting by the anticipated event proportion.
  • Why this design: EPV is a resource-planning rule of thumb rather than a complete calculation for power or prediction error. Develop the protocol further using explicit performance and shrinkage assumptions such as those in Section 6.5.
  • Formula: \[n_{events} = EPV \times k, \quad n_{subjects} = n_{events} / \pi\] Peduzzi et al. (1996), J Clin Epidemiol 49(12), 1373-1379.
res_6_7 <- calculate("predictiveModel", "plan", "events", n_parameters = 10, epv = 10, event_prevalence = 0.30)
print(res_6_7)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Prediction model development (events-per-variable)"
#> • Required sample size: 334
#> • Events required: 100
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • n_parameters = candidate predictor parameters (k)
#> • epv = events per variable (classic minimum 10)
#> • event_prevalence = proportion of subjects with the outcome
#> ! EPV >= 10 is a minimum heuristic; Riley et al. (2019, BMJ 364:l951)
#> ! provide a modern precision-based alternative (planned for a later release).
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n_events = EPV * k ; n_subjects = n_events / prevalence`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n_{events} = EPV \times k, \quad n_{subjects} = n_{events} / \pi$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Specify candidate predictor parameters k = 10, Events Per Variable
#> target EPV = 10.
#> • Step 2: Calculate required events: n_events = EPV * k = 10 * 10 = 100.
#> • Step 3: Convert to subjects using event prevalence pi = 0.30: n_subjects =
#> n_events / prevalence = 334.
#> • Step 4: Required events = 100, Total subjects = 334.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Peduzzi, P., Concato, J., Kemper, E., Holford, T. R., & Feinstein, A. R. (1996). A simulation study of the number of events per variable in logistic regression analysis. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 49(12), 1373-1379.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and recruitment: Target 100 events, giving 334 patients by the assumed event proportion. This targets an expected event count; actual observed events can still fall short and need consideration in accrual and follow-up planning.

6.8 Inter-Rater Reliability: Cohen’s Kappa Precision

  • Population and decision: Two radiologists estimate binary reading agreement in a prespecified breast-imaging assessment set designed to have approximately balanced positive and negative reading margins.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Readers independently assess the same images while blinded to each other’s decisions. Each patient forms a pair of ratings; κ measures agreement beyond chance, not sensitivity or specificity.
  • Planning inputs: Use balanced pi1 = pi2 = 0.50, anticipated kappa = 0.70, and 95% CI half-width d = 0.10. Actual margins require evidence from the target population or an explicit enrichment strategy.
  • Why this design: This estimates one κ with two fixed readers. The unit is the patient/specimen being rated; repeating the same image does not replace independent specimens.
  • Formula (Cantor 1996): \[n = Q\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{d}\right)^2, \quad Q = \frac{p_o(1-p_o)}{(1-p_e)^2}\] 
res_6_8 <- calculate("kappa", "estimate", "proportion", pi1 = 0.50, pi2 = 0.50, kappa = 0.70, d = 0.10, alpha = 0.05)
print(res_6_8)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Cohen's kappa estimation (CI precision)"
#> • Required sample size: 196
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • pi1/pi2 = expected Rating-1 proportions for rater 1 / rater 2
#> • kappa1 = planning value of kappa
#> • d = desired CI half-width
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = Q * (z/d)^2; Q is the full asymptotic variance factor from Cantor (1996),
#> Eq 3`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = Q\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{d}\right)^2, \quad Q = n\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\kappa})\;\text{(Cantor Eq. 3)}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Cohen's kappa estimation (CI precision).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: pi1 = 0.50, pi2 = 0.50, kappa = 0.70, d = 0.10,
#> alpha = 0.05, Q = 0.51.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: n = Q * (z/d)^2; Q is the full asymptotic
#> variance factor from Cantor (1996), Eq 3.
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Required sample size: 196; Total
#> sample size: 196.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Cantor, A. B. (1996). Sample-size calculations for Cohen's kappa. Psychological Methods, 1(2), 150-153 (Fleiss-Cohen-Everitt 1969 asymptotic variance; worked examples N=165 and N=214).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and workload: 196 independent specimens, each assessed by both readers, giving 392 readings. This result concerns the balanced assessment set; different rating margins require their own planning.

6.9 Inter-Rater Reliability: Two Independent Kappa Test

  • Population and decision: An imaging department compares a structured reporting checklist with routine reading using independent patient image sets for the two workflows, with two readers producing paired ratings within each set.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Estimate a κ in each group, then compare the independent estimates. Reusing the same images under both workflows creates dependent κ estimates and is not the design modeled here.
  • Planning inputs: Assume κ values 0.70 and 0.50, margins of 0.50, two-sided α=0.05, and 80% power. The required number refers to specimens per group, not to the number of radiologists.
  • Why this design: Keep case spectrum, reader training, and category definitions comparable between groups so the comparison reflects the intended reporting workflow difference.
  • Formula: \[n = \frac{\left[z_{\alpha}\sqrt{2Q_1} + z_{\beta}\sqrt{Q_1+Q_2}\right]^2}{(K_1-K_2)^2}\] Cantor (1996), Psychological Methods 1(2), 150-153.
res_6_9 <- calculate("kappa", "test", "proportion", pi1 = 0.50, pi2 = 0.50, kappa1 = 0.70, kappa2 = 0.50, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_6_9)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Cohen's kappa test (two independent kappas)"
#> • Required sample size: 214
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • pi1/pi2 = expected Rating-1 proportions (both raters/groups)
#> • kappa1 = kappa under the null (e.g. questionnaire 1)
#> • kappa2 = kappa under the alternative (e.g. questionnaire 2)
#> • n is per group (two independent kappa estimates)
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `n = (z_a*sqrt(2*Q1) + z_b*sqrt(Q1+Q2))^2/(K1-K2)^2`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$n = \frac{\left[z_{\alpha}\sqrt{2Q_1} + z_{\beta}\sqrt{Q_1+Q_2}\right]^2}{(K_1-K_2)^2}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Cohen's kappa test (two independent kappas).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: pi1 = 0.50, pi2 = 0.50, kappa1 = 0.70, kappa2 =
#> 0.50, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80, Q_null = 0.51, Q_alt = 0.75.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: n = (z_a*sqrt(2*Q1) +
#> z_b*sqrt(Q1+Q2))^2/(K1-K2)^2.
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Required sample size: 214; Total
#> sample size: 214.
#> Reference:
#> Primary: Cantor, A. B. (1996). Sample-size calculations for Cohen's kappa. Psychological Methods, 1(2), 150-153 (worked example: K1=0.7, K2=0.5, pi=0.5 -> N=214).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and workload: 214 specimens per group, 428 total. Two ratings per specimen imply about 856 interpretations across the study.

6.10 Interrupted Time Series (ITS Level Change)

  • Population and decision: A hospital implements an antimicrobial stewardship policy on a defined date, using 12 monthly observations before and 12 after implementation to assess an immediate level change.
  • Procedures and endpoint: Each time point is a hospital-level aggregate, such as antibiotic-use intensity per hundred patient-days. Monthly dependence matters; patients contributing to a month are not independent time points in this calculation.
  • Planning inputs: Assume a change of 2 residual outcome SDs, effect_sd = 2, AR(1) correlation rho = 0.30, and n_pre = n_post = 12. This is a strong illustrative standardized effect, not a 2% reduction.
  • Why this design: This evaluates approximate power for a fixed time series using a simplified level-shift and AR(1) adjustment. Seasonality, pre-existing trends, slope changes, or concurrent policies need appropriate segmented-regression or simulation planning.
  • Formula (AR(1)-adjusted approximation): \[\text{power} = \Phi\left(\frac{\delta}{SE} - z_{\alpha/2}\right), \quad SE = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n_{eff}^{pre}} + \tfrac{1}{n_{eff}^{post}}}, \quad n_{eff} = \frac{n(1-\rho)}{1+\rho}\] Bernal, Cummins & Gasparrini (2017), Int J Epidemiol 46(1), 348-355 (experimental approximation).
res_6_10 <- calculate("its", "test", "rate", effect_sd = 2, n_pre = 12, n_post = 12, rho = 0.3, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8)
print(res_6_10)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Results
#> • Design type: "Interrupted time series (level change, AR(1)-adjusted)"
#> • Power achieved: 0.949
#> Parameter roles
#> 
#> • effect_sd = anticipated level change in outcome SD units
#> • n_pre/n_post = number of time points before/after the interruption
#> • rho = AR(1) autocorrelation of the series
#> ! EXPERIMENTAL method: transparent AR(1)-adjusted normal approximation.
#> ! Bernal et al. (2017, Int J Epidemiol) recommend >= 8 time points per segment;
#> ! rigorous ITS power calculations require simulation.
#> 
#> Formula (plain text):
#> `power = Phi(effect/SE - z); SE = sqrt(1/n_eff_pre + 1/n_eff_post); n_eff =
#> n(1-rho)/(1+rho)`
#> Formula (LaTeX):
#> $$\text{power} = \Phi\left(\frac{\delta}{SE} - z_{\alpha/2}\right), \quad SE = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n_{eff}^{pre}} + \tfrac{1}{n_{eff}^{post}}}$$
#> Calculation process:
#> 
#> • Step 1: Identify study design: Interrupted time series (level change,
#> AR(1)-adjusted).
#> • Step 2: Input parameters: effect_sd = 2, n_pre = 12, n_post = 12, rho = 0.30,
#> alpha = 0.05.
#> • Step 3: Apply design formula: power = Phi(effect/SE - z); SE =
#> sqrt(1/n_eff_pre + 1/n_eff_post); n_eff = n(1-rho)/(1+rho).
#> • Step 4: Calculated sample size metrics: Power achieved: 0.949.
#> Reference:
#> Framework: Bernal, J. L., Cummins, S., & Gasparrini, A. (2017). Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial. International Journal of Epidemiology, 46(1), 348-355. Sample-size content is a transparent approximation, not from a validated source.
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
  • Result and observation plan: Approximate power for the 24 monthly observations is 94.9%. This does not mean 24 patients are required or that seasonality and time trends are controlled; align observation length with the intended model and data quality.

Chapter 7: Protocol Writing & Visual Diagnostics

Turning the scenarios into complete protocols

Protocol A: BP trial assumptions and recruitment sensitivity

Record the Section 1.1 population, week-12 change endpoint, and independent-patient analysis unit together. Identify the supporting study, its sample size, mean changes, and change-score SD. A source reporting only baseline SD or a standard error does not directly provide the planning SD.

The table holds the control mean at 10, two-sided α=0.05, and power at 80%, while increasing SD from 3 to 4 or reducing the group difference from 2 to 1.5. Recruitment is separately inflated for 10% missing primary outcomes, illustrating the impact of plausible uncertainty on the budget.

rct_plan <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Base case", "Higher variability", "Smaller difference", "Both changes"),
  mean2 = c(12, 12, 11.5, 11.5),
  sd = c(3, 4, 3, 4)
)
rct_plan$complete <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(rct_plan)), function(i) {
  calculate("rct", "test", "mean",
    mean1 = 10, mean2 = rct_plan$mean2[i], sd = rct_plan$sd[i]
  )$n_per_group
}, numeric(1))
rct_plan$recruit <- ceiling(rct_plan$complete / 0.9)
knitr::kable(rct_plan,
  col.names = c("Scenario", "Study mean", "Change SD", "Complete/arm", "Recruit/arm")
)
Scenario Study mean Change SD Complete/arm Recruit/arm
Base case 12.0 3 37 42
Higher variability 12.0 4 64 72
Smaller difference 11.5 3 64 72
Both changes 11.5 4 113 126

State which scenario drives the final target, why it is appropriate, and whether recruitment and endpoint capacity can support it. Merely stating that inputs came from the literature obscures differences in populations and measurements.

Protocol B: Sensitivity case quotas and screening capacity

Section 5.1 requires 196 evaluable disease-positive cases, whereas a referral service initially sees patients of unknown disease status. Estimate source prevalence from consecutive records using the same referral criteria before translating the case target into examination capacity.

The table compares prevalence assumptions of 10%, 20%, and 30%, showing expectation-based conversion and the minimum enrollment for 90% probability of enough cases. The 95% confidence level for sensitivity and the 90% recruitment-yield probability are separate quantities.

diag_plan <- data.frame(prevalence = c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30))
diag_plan$expected <- ceiling(
  res_5_1$target_state_cases_needed / diag_plan$prevalence
)
diag_plan$guaranteed <- vapply(diag_plan$prevalence, function(prev) {
  screen_required(res_5_1$target_state_cases_needed, prev, beta = 0.10)
}, numeric(1))
knitr::kable(diag_plan,
  col.names = c("Prevalence", "Expectation-based total", "90% yield requirement")
)
Prevalence Expectation-based total 90% yield requirement
0.1 1960 2132
0.2 980 1061
0.3 654 704

These targets refer to participants completing both index and reference assessments. Define reference-test capacity, repeat specimens, and monthly throughput. If only 95% of invitees complete both assessments, treating the table as an invitation count does not preserve the original case-yield guarantee.

Protocol text to adapt

RCT example. This parallel, blinded, randomized trial evaluates baseline-to-week-12 systolic BP reduction. Based on [insert compatible evidence source], anticipated reductions are 10 and 12 mmHg with common change-score SD 3 mmHg. Two-sided α=0.05 and 80% power require 37 analyzable patients per arm using two-sample t-test planning. Allowing 10% missing primary endpoints, we plan 42 per arm, 84 total. Calculations use SampleSizeCalc; the primary analysis population and missing-outcome handling are prespecified in the analysis plan.

Diagnostic example. Consecutive patients from [insert intended referral setting] undergo a locked-threshold index test and a common reference examination. Based on [insert compatible evidence sources], anticipated sensitivity is 85% and prevalence 20%. Estimating sensitivity with approximately 0.05 half-width at 95% confidence requires 196 evaluable cases. A minimum 1061 complete participants gives at least 90% probability of enough cases under the binomial prevalence assumption. Procedures for incomplete reference assessments and supplementary recruitment are prespecified separately.

Detailed reports and plots

Default print() output includes both formula formats, the calculation process, and references. Use summary() to additionally display all input parameters, design axes, and recorded adjustments:

summary(res_1_1)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Sample Size Calculation Summary
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Study Design
#> • Type: "Two independent samples, mean comparison"
#> • Design: "rct"
#> • Task: "test" | Outcome: "mean"
#> 
#> ── Parameters
#> • mean1: 10
#> • mean2: 12
#> • sd: 3
#> • alpha: 0.05
#> • power: 0.8
#> 
#> ── Sample Size Results
#> • Sample size per group: 37
#> • Total sample size: 74
#> 
#> ── Formula
#> Plain text:
#> `n = 2 * ((Z_alpha/2 + Z_beta) * sd / (mean1 - mean2))^2`
#> LaTeX:
#> $$n = 2\left(\frac{Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}}{\delta}\right)^2 = 2\left(\frac{(Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta}) \cdot \sigma}{\mu_1 - \mu_2}\right)^2$$
#> 
#> ── Calculation Process
#> • Step 1: State hypotheses: H0: mu1 = mu2 vs H1: mu1 != mu2 (two-sided alpha =
#> 0.05, power = 0.80).
#> • Step 2: Calculate mean difference delta = |mu1 - mu2| = |10 - 12| = 2; common
#> SD sigma = 3.
#> • Step 3: Determine critical values: Z_(alpha/2) = 1.96 (for two-sided alpha =
#> 0.05), Z_beta = 0.8416 (for power = 0.80).
#> • Step 4: Compute initial sample size via normal approximation: n0 = 2 *
#> ((Z_(alpha/2) + Z_beta) * sigma / delta)^2 = 2 * ((1.96 + 0.8416) * 3 / 2)^2 =
#> 35.32.
#> • Step 5: Refine via exact two-sample Student's t-test power iteration
#> (accounting for degrees of freedom df = 2n - 2).
#> • Step 6: Round up to integer: n = 37 per group, total sample size N = 74.
#> 
#> ── Reference
#> Chow, S. C., Shao, J., Wang, H., & Lokhnygina, Y. (2017). Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Chapter 3 (Comparing Means), Section 3.2.1 two-sample parallel design, Eq 3.11 (p. 48; the Student t refinement is Table 3.2, p. 49).
#> 
#>  Also: Machin et al. (2018) Eq 5.4, p. 69 (same formula with the Student t correction term).
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
plot(res_1_1, type = "power")

plot(res_1_1, type = "sample_size")
